# Marmotta

[![CI](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Latest release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/napi-bindings/marmotta)](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/releases/latest) [![marmotta monthly downloads on npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/dm/marmotta?label=marmotta%20downloads)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/marmotta) [![@napi-bindings/marmotta monthly downloads on npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/dm/%40napi-bindings%2Fmarmotta?label=%40napi-bindings%2Fmarmotta%20downloads)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@napi-bindings/marmotta)
Marmotta builds Node.js native addons written in C or C++ with [Node-API](https://nodejs.org/api/n-api.html). It uses [Zig](https://ziglang.org/) as the compiler toolchain and can install Zig for you, so projects do not need to configure `node-gyp` or CMake. ## Contents - [Highlights](#highlights) - [Requirements](#requirements) - [Installation](#installation) - [Quick start](#quick-start) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Command-line reference](#command-line-reference) - [Zig toolchain](#zig-toolchain) - [Contributing](#contributing) - [License](#license) - [Team](#team) - [Contributors](#contributors) ## Highlights - Build C and C++ Node-API addons into `.node` files. - Use the Node-API headers supplied by Marmotta; no separate Node header installation is needed. - Reuse node-gyp-oriented sources that use `NODE_GYP_MODULE_NAME`. - Build for the host platform or pass a Zig target triple for cross-compilation. - Install Zig automatically when a suitable compiler is not already on `PATH`. - Use a Zig installation that already exists on the system with `MARMOTTA_ZIG_DIR`, for example where downloads are blocked. - Load the same addon in Node.js, Electron, Deno, and Bun. On Windows, Marmotta binds Node-API functions to the process that loads the addon instead of to `node.exe`, so no delay-load hook is needed. ## Requirements - Node.js 20 or later and npm. To run Marmotta without Node.js, use a [standalone binary](#standalone-binary) instead. - A C or C++ Node-API addon source file (`.c`, `.cc`, `.cpp`, or `.cxx`). - `tar` and internet access when Marmotta needs to download Zig. Automatic Zig downloads are supported on x64 and ARM64 Linux, macOS, and Windows hosts. On other host platforms, install Zig separately and make it available on `PATH`. ## Installation Install the unscoped package globally: ```sh npm install --global marmotta marmotta --help ``` Or add Marmotta to a project and run it with `npx`: ```sh npm install --save-dev marmotta npx marmotta --help ``` The same CLI is also published as `@napi-bindings/marmotta`. To install that package instead: ```sh npm install --save-dev @napi-bindings/marmotta npx marmotta --help ``` ### Standalone binary Every release ships a self-contained executable per platform. It embeds the CLI and the Node-API headers, so Node.js and npm are not required to run it; Zig is still downloaded on first use, exactly as with the npm package. 1. Download the file for your platform from the [GitHub releases page](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/releases), for example `marmotta-v0.10.0-linux-x64`. 2. Make it executable and put it on your `PATH`: ```sh chmod +x marmotta-v0.10.0-linux-x64 sudo mv marmotta-v0.10.0-linux-x64 /usr/local/bin/marmotta marmotta --version ``` On Windows, rename the file to `marmotta.exe` and place it in a directory on `PATH`. | File | Platform | | --- | --- | | `marmotta-vX.Y.Z-linux-x64` | Linux x64 (glibc) | | `marmotta-vX.Y.Z-linux-arm64` | Linux ARM64 (glibc) | | `marmotta-vX.Y.Z-linux-x64-musl` | Linux x64 (musl, e.g. Alpine) | | `marmotta-vX.Y.Z-linux-arm64-musl` | Linux ARM64 (musl, e.g. Alpine) | | `marmotta-vX.Y.Z-darwin-x64` | macOS, Intel | | `marmotta-vX.Y.Z-darwin-arm64` | macOS, Apple silicon | | `marmotta-vX.Y.Z-windows-x64.exe` | Windows x64 | | `marmotta-vX.Y.Z-windows-arm64.exe` | Windows ARM64 | Each release includes a `SHA256SUMS` file and GitHub build provenance attestations, so a download can be checked with `sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS` and `gh attestation verify`. Notes on the standalone binaries: - They behave like the npm package: `NODE_OPTIONS` does not affect them, and a stray `.env` or `bunfig.toml` in the project directory does not change what they do. Like any Bun program, they do honor `BUN_OPTIONS`. - The macOS binaries carry an ad-hoc signature with the hardened runtime enabled and the JIT entitlements JavaScriptCore needs; they are not notarized. If macOS blocks a downloaded binary, remove the quarantine attribute with `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ` (or control-click and open it). - The musl binaries link against `libstdc++`, which a stock Alpine image does not ship. Install it first: `apk add libstdc++`. - The binaries are built with [`bun build --compile`](https://bun.com/docs/bundler/executables). ### Package managers Each release also ships native packages for Linux, built from the standalone executables, so Node.js and npm are not required: | Package | Platform | Install | | --- | --- | --- | | `.deb` | Debian, Ubuntu | `sudo apt install ./marmotta__amd64.deb` | | `.rpm` | Fedora, RHEL | `sudo dnf install ./marmotta--1.x86_64.rpm` | | `.apk` | Alpine | `sudo apk add --allow-untrusted ./marmotta--r0.x86_64.apk` | | `.pkg.tar.zst` | Arch Linux | `sudo pacman -U ./marmotta--1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst` | The ARM64 variants use the same names with `arm64`/`aarch64` in place of `amd64`/`x86_64`. Download them from the [releases page](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/releases). Homebrew, AUR, Nix, Scoop, and winget recipes are generated for every release and included in `marmotta-v-packaging.tar.gz`; see [`packaging/README.md`](packaging/README.md) for the publishing and installation instructions. ## Quick start Create a Node.js project with a C or C++ Node-API source file. For example, save this as `src/hello.c`: ```c #include #include static napi_value Hello(napi_env env, napi_callback_info info) { napi_value result; napi_status status = napi_create_string_utf8(env, "world", 5, &result); assert(status == napi_ok); return result; } static napi_value Initialize(napi_env env, napi_value exports) { napi_property_descriptor descriptor = { "hello", 0, Hello, 0, 0, 0, napi_default, 0 }; napi_status status = napi_define_properties(env, exports, 1, &descriptor); assert(status == napi_ok); return exports; } NAPI_MODULE(NODE_GYP_MODULE_NAME, Initialize) ``` Create `marmotta.config.json` in the project root: ```json { "name": "hello", "sources": ["src/hello.c"], "outputDir": "build" } ``` Build and load the addon: ```sh npx marmotta build node -e "console.log(require('./build/hello.node').hello())" ``` The example prints `world`. `configure` can be run to validate the project and prepare Zig before building, but it is optional; `build` loads the configuration and ensures the toolchain itself. ## Configuration All paths in either configuration file are resolved relative to the project directory. The configuration file is optional. Without it, Marmotta uses the package or directory name, discovers source files, and places the addon in the project root. You can use `marmotta.config.js` to compute configuration values with JavaScript. If both config files are present, `marmotta.config.js` takes precedence over `marmotta.config.json`. Export either a configuration object as the default export or a function that returns one; the function may be asynchronous and receives the project directory, requested Zig target, and host platform and architecture: ```js export default ({ target, platform }) => { const isWindows = target ? target.includes('windows') : platform === 'win32'; return { name: 'hello', sources: ['src/hello.c'], cFlags: isWindows ? ['-DWIN32_BUILD'] : [], }; }; ``` For `.js` files, use the module format selected by your project's `package.json` (`"type": "module"` for ESM). JavaScript configuration files execute as project code. | Field | Type | Default | Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `name` | string | `package.json` name, or project directory name | Addon name, also used in the output filename `.node`. Characters other than letters, digits, `_`, and `-` are replaced with `_`. | | `sources` | string array | discovered source files | C/C++ sources to compile. An empty or omitted array enables recursive discovery. | | `includeDirs` | string array | `[]` | Additional header search directories. | | `cFlags` | string array | `[]` | Additional compiler flags for C sources. | | `cxxFlags` | string array | `[]` | Additional compiler flags for C++ sources. | | `linkerFlags` | string array | `[]` | Additional linker flags. | | `outputDir` | string | `.` | Output directory. The generated addon is `/.node`. | | `zigVersion` | string | Zig from `PATH`, else local/latest stable | Pin an exact stable Zig version, for example `0.14.1`. When set, Marmotta uses or downloads this managed version instead of using Zig from `PATH`. Ignored when `MARMOTTA_ZIG_DIR` is set. | Each array field must contain only strings. During source discovery Marmotta ignores `.git`, `.marmotta`, `build`, `dist`, and `node_modules`. Explicit source and include paths must be relative to the project directory or absolute paths; each source must exist and be a file. Marmotta defines `NODE_GYP_MODULE_NAME` for every source file using the configured addon name. Characters that cannot appear in a C identifier are replaced with `_`, and a leading digit is prefixed with `_`. This allows compatible sources to use `NODE_API_MODULE(NODE_GYP_MODULE_NAME, Initialize)` without changing the macro. ## Command-line reference Run `marmotta --help` or `npx marmotta --help` for the built-in usage summary. ### Commands | Command | Description | | --- | --- | | `marmotta configure` | Validate the project configuration and ensure Zig is available. | | `marmotta build` | Compile the configured or discovered C/C++ sources into a `.node` addon. | | `marmotta rebuild` | Remove the selected generated addon and build it again. | | `marmotta clean` | Remove the generated addon file only. Zig and other build files are left untouched. | | `marmotta install` | Ensure a Zig compiler is available, downloading one if needed. | | `marmotta list` | List Zig versions managed by Marmotta. | | `marmotta remove ` | Remove a managed Zig version, for example `marmotta remove 0.14.1`. | ### Options | Option | Commands | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `-C, --directory ` | `configure`, `build`, `rebuild`, `clean` | Project directory. Defaults to the current working directory. | | `-o, --output-dir ` | `build`, `rebuild`, `clean` | Override `outputDir`. Relative paths are resolved from the project directory. | | `--target ` | `build`, `rebuild` | Zig target triple used for cross-compilation. | | `--debug` | `build`, `rebuild` | Compile without optimization and include debug information (`-O0 -g` instead of `-O2`). | | `--json` | Any command | Emit machine-readable JSON Lines instead of plain text. Recognized before or after the command. | | `-h, --help` | Any command | Show help. | | `-v, --version` | Top-level command | Show the Marmotta version. | For example, request a build for ARM64 macOS: ```sh npx marmotta build --target aarch64-macos ``` Use `--json` in CI when another process needs to consume Marmotta's output; see [Logging](#logging) for the record format and the `MARMOTTA_LOG` variable. Use a target triple supported by Zig for the intended target. Cross-compilation does not run the resulting addon on the host; load it on a compatible target system. ### Logging By default Marmotta writes plain text: command results on stdout and errors on stderr, with no level prefixes, so scripts that read `marmotta --version` or `marmotta list` keep working unchanged. Pass `--json` when another process needs to consume the output, as in CI. The flag is recognized before or after the command, and each record is one JSON object on its own line (JSON Lines): ```sh npx marmotta build --json npx marmotta --json list ``` ```json {"level":"info","time":1730000000000,"message":"Addon built: /project/build/hello.node"} {"level":"info","time":1730000000001,"data":{"versions":["0.13.0","0.14.0"]},"message":"Installed Zig versions"} {"level":"error","time":1730000000002,"data":{"code":"CLI_ARGUMENT_ERROR","exitCode":2},"message":"Unknown option: --bogus"} ``` - `level` is a string such as `info`, `warn`, or `error`. Informational records go to stdout; warnings and errors go to stderr. - `message` is the human-readable text, and `data` carries the record's structured context when there is any, such as the error `code` and `exitCode`, the installed `versions`, or a child process's `command` and `stream`. - Command results, such as help, the version, `list`, confirmations and error messages, are always printed. Output from the Zig and `tar` child processes is captured and re-emitted as records tagged with `command` and `stream`, so every line printed in `--json` mode is valid JSON and compiler errors are never hidden. Lines from the child's stderr are `warn` records on stderr; lines from its stdout are `info` records on stdout. Lines keep their order within each stream, but the order between a child's stdout and stderr lines is not preserved. - Set `MARMOTTA_LOG` to the minimum level for diagnostic records: `trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, `fatal`, or `silent`. The default is `info`, which hides `debug` records: which Zig is used, where Zig is downloaded from, and each Zig or `tar` command line. An unrecognized value is ignored with a warning. `MARMOTTA_LOG` filters diagnostics only; it never hides a command's result or its final error. It applies to both formats and does not change the shape of the output. `--version` is a top-level request and cannot be combined with a command, so `marmotta build --version` fails with an argument error instead of printing the version and skipping the build. ## Zig toolchain Without a `zigVersion` pin, Marmotta uses `zig` from `PATH` when available, then a locally managed version, and otherwise downloads the latest stable Zig release for the supported host platform into the Marmotta home directory (see [Marmotta home directory](#marmotta-home-directory)). If `zigVersion` is set, Marmotta ignores `PATH` and selects that exact managed version, downloading it if necessary. If the pinned version is not available for the host platform, the command fails instead of falling back to another version. If the download index includes a checksum, Marmotta verifies the downloaded archive. If `MARMOTTA_ZIG_DIR` is set, Marmotta uses only that Zig and never downloads one (see [Existing Zig installation](#existing-zig-installation)). Prepare Zig in advance: ```sh npx marmotta install ``` List and remove toolchain versions managed by Marmotta: ```sh npx marmotta list npx marmotta remove 0.10.0 ``` `list` and `remove` operate only on versions managed by Marmotta; they do not list, uninstall, or modify a system Zig executable found on `PATH`. ### Existing Zig installation Set `MARMOTTA_ZIG_DIR` to the directory of a Zig installation that already exists on the system, for example when downloads are blocked or the toolchain is provided by the organization and cannot be changed: ```sh export MARMOTTA_ZIG_DIR=/opt/zig-x86_64-linux-0.14.1 npx marmotta build ``` - The directory must contain the Zig executable (`zig`, or `zig.exe` on Windows), as in the archives published on ziglang.org. - Marmotta uses this Zig for every command and never downloads Zig while the variable is set. It takes precedence over Zig on `PATH` and over the versions managed by Marmotta, and a `zigVersion` pin in the configuration is ignored. - If the directory does not contain a Zig executable that can be run, the command fails with `MARMOTTA_ZIG_DIR_UNAVAILABLE` and names the expected path. Marmotta does not fall back to another Zig. - The value follows the same rules as `MARMOTTA_HOME`: it must be an absolute path without leading or trailing whitespace, otherwise it is rejected with `MARMOTTA_ZIG_DIR_INVALID`. An empty value is treated as unset. - Marmotta never writes to this directory, and `list` and `remove` do not include or change it. Temporary build files still go to the Marmotta home directory, and Zig's global cache follows the rules described there. ### Marmotta home directory Marmotta stores managed Zig toolchains (`toolchains/zig/`) and temporary build files in its home directory. By default this is `.marmotta` in the user's home directory (`~/.marmotta` on Unix-like systems or `%USERPROFILE%\.marmotta` on Windows). Set `MARMOTTA_HOME` to use another directory, for example when the home directory is read-only or not persistent, as on restricted CI runners or in containers: ```sh export MARMOTTA_HOME=/var/cache/marmotta npx marmotta build ``` - The value must be an absolute path. On Windows it must start with a drive letter (`D:\marmotta`) or be a UNC path (`\\server\share\marmotta`); root-relative paths such as `\marmotta` and device paths such as `\\?\` or `\\.\` are not accepted. `~` is not expanded, and values with leading or trailing whitespace are rejected instead of being trimmed. Invalid values are rejected with `MARMOTTA_HOME_INVALID`. - An empty value is treated as unset. - Marmotta creates the directory, and the subdirectories it needs, when a command first writes to it. If a directory cannot be created or written, for example when building, the command fails with `MARMOTTA_HOME_UNAVAILABLE` and names the directory and the cause. A failed Zig installation keeps its `ZIG_INSTALL_FAILED` code and includes the same details. Commands that write nothing, such as `marmotta list`, or `configure` and `install` when Zig is already available, also work with a read-only directory. - When `MARMOTTA_HOME` is set, Zig's global cache is placed in `/cache`, so builds do not write to the home directory. If `ZIG_GLOBAL_CACHE_DIR` is already set to a non-empty value, Marmotta leaves it unchanged. Without `MARMOTTA_HOME`, Marmotta does not change the cache location and Zig uses its own default. - Marmotta only removes files and directories it created, such as a Zig version removed with `marmotta remove` or temporary build directories. It never deletes or cleans the `MARMOTTA_HOME` directory itself, so it can point to a shared location. ## Contributing Bug reports, documentation improvements, and code contributions are welcome. See the [contributing guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) for project contribution and review guidelines. ## License Marmotta is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) for the full license text. ## Team - [Nicola Del Gobbo](https://github.com/NickNaso) ## Contributors - [Simone Russo](https://github.com/ErRusso)

docs.markdown: # Contributing To Marmotta Thank you for taking an interest in contributing to Marmotta. We are excited to receive your support and knowledge. This guide is our attempt to help you help us. > ## Note > This is an informal guide. For full details, please review the formal > [CONTRIBUTING > document](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) > and our [Developer Certificate of > Origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developer_Certificate_of_Origin). ## Table Of Contents - [Table Of Contents](#table-of-contents) - [Types Of Contributions We're Looking For](#types-of-contributions-were-looking-for) - [Ground Rules & Expectations](#ground-rules--expectations) - [How To Contribute](#how-to-contribute) - [Setting Up Your Environment](#setting-up-your-environment) ## Types Of Contributions We're Looking For In short, we welcome any type of contribution you are willing to provide. No contribution is too small. We gladly accept contributions such as: * Documentation improvements: from small typo corrections to major document reworks * Helping others by answering questions in pull requests and issues * Fixing [known bugs](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3Abug) * Reporting previously unknown bugs by opening an issue with a minimal reproduction ## Ground Rules & Expectations Before we get started, here are a few things we expect from you (and that you should expect from others): * Be respectful and thoughtful in your conversations around this project. This project is maintained by a diverse set of people from all across the globe. Each person has their own views and opinions about the project. Try to listen to each other and reach an agreement or compromise. * We have a [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). You must adhere to it to participate in this project. * If you open a pull request, please ensure your contribution passes all tests. If there are test failures, you will need to address them before we can merge your contribution. ## How To Contribute If you'd like to contribute, start by searching through the [issues](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/issues) and [pull requests](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/pulls) to see whether someone else has raised a similar idea or question. If you don't see your idea listed, and you think it fits into the goals of this guide, do one of the following: * **If your contribution is minor,** such as a typo fix, open a pull request. * **If your contribution is major,** such as a new feature, start by opening an issue first. That way, other people can weigh in on the discussion before you do any work. ## Setting Up Your Environment Please adhere to the project's code and [documentation](./style-guide.md) style. Some popular tools that automatically "correct" code and documentation do not follow a style that conforms to this project's styles.

# Marmotta Style Guide

## Welcome

Welcome to *Marmotta Style Guide*. This guide is here to provide you with a
conventional writing style for users writing developer documentation on our Open
Source framework. Each topic is precise and well explained to help you write
documentation users can easily understand and implement.

## Who is this guide for?

This guide is for anyone who loves to build with Marmotta or wants to contribute
to our documentation. You do not need to be an expert in writing technical
documentation. This guide is here to help you.

Read the [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
file on GitHub to join our Open Source folks.

## Before you write

You need to know the following:

* JavaScript
* TypeScript
* Node.js
* Git
* GitHub
* Markdown
* HTTP
* NPM

### Consider your Audience

Before you start writing, think about your audience. In this case, your audience
should already know, JavaScript, NPM, Node.js and native addon. It is necessary
to keep your readers in mind because they are the ones consuming your content. 
You want to give as much useful information as possible. Consider the vital
things they need to know and how they can understand them. Use words and 
references that readers can relate to easily. Ask for feedback from the 
community, it can help you write better documentation that focuses on the user
and what you want to achieve.

### Get straight to the point

Give your readers a clear and precise action to take. Start with what is most
important. This way, you can help them find what they need faster. Mostly,
readers tend to read the first content on a page, and many will not scroll
further.

**Example**

Less like this: Colons are very important to register a parametric path. It lets
the framework know there is a new parameter created. You can place the colon
before the parameter name so the parametric path can be created.

More Like this: To register a parametric path, put a colon before the parameter
name. Using a colon lets the framework know it is a parametric path and not a
static path.

### Avoid adding video or image content


Do not add videos or screenshots to the documentation. It is easier to keep
under version control. Videos and images will eventually end up becoming
outdated as new updates keep developing. Instead, make a referral link or a
YouTube video. You can add links by using `[Title](https://www.websitename.com)`
in the markdown.

### Avoid plagiarism

Make sure you avoid copying other people's work. Keep it as original as
possible. You can learn from what they have done and reference where it is from
if you use a particular quote from their work.


## Word Choice

There are a few things you need to use and avoid when writing your documentation
to improve readability for readers and make documentation neat, direct, and
clean.


### When to use the second person "you" as the pronoun

When writing articles or guides, your content should communicate directly to
readers in the second person ("you") addressed form. It is easier to give them
direct instruction on what to do on a particular topic.

**Example**

Less like this: we can use the following functions.

More like this: You can use the following functions.

> According to [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You), ***You*** is usually a second person pronoun.
> Also, used to refer to an indeterminate person, as a more common alternative
> to a very formal indefinite pronoun.

### When to avoid the second person "you" as the pronoun

One of the main rules of formal writing such as reference documentation, or API
documentation, is to avoid the second person ("you") or directly addressing the
reader.

**Example**

Less like this: You can use the following recommendation as an example.

More like this: As an example, the following recommendations should be
referenced.

### Avoid using contractions

Contractions are the shortened version of written and spoken forms of a word,
i.e. using "don't" instead of "do not". Avoid contractions to provide a more
formal tone.

### Avoid using condescending terms

Condescending terms are words that include:

* Just
* Easy
* Simply
* Basically
* Obviously

Not everyone who reads the documentation has the same level of understanding.

### Starting with a verb

Mostly start your description with a verb, which makes it simple and precise for
the reader to follow. Prefer using present tense because it is easier to read
and understand than the past or future tense.

**Example**

 Less like this: There is a need for Node.js to be installed before you can be
 able to use Marmotta.

 More like this: Install Node.js to make use of Marmotta.

### Grammatical moods

Grammatical moods are a great way to express your writing. Avoid sounding too
bossy while making a direct statement. Know when to switch between indicative,
imperative, and subjunctive moods.


**Indicative** - Use when making a factual statement or question.

Example: Since there is no testing framework available, "Marmotta recommends ways
to write tests".

**Imperative** - Use when giving instructions, actions, commands, or when you
write your headings.

Example: Install dependencies before starting development.


**Subjunctive** -  Use when making suggestions, hypotheses, or non-factual
statements.

### Use **active** voice instead of **passive**

Using active voice is a more compact and direct way of conveying your
documentation.

**Example**

Passive: The node dependencies and packages are installed by npm.

Active:  npm installs packages and node dependencies.

## Writing Style

### Documentation titles

When creating a new guide, API, or reference in the `/docs/` directory, use
short titles that best describe the topic of your documentation. Name your files
in kebab-cases and avoid Raw or camelCase. To learn more about kebab-case you
can visit this medium article on [Case
Styles](https://medium.com/better-programming/string-case-styles-camel-pascal-snake-and-kebab-case-981407998841).

**Examples**:

>`adding-test.md`,

 `removing-requests.md`.

### Hyperlinks

Hyperlinks should have a clear title of what they reference.

For example: [Marmotta contributing guide](../CONTRIBUTING.md).

Include in your documentation as many essential references as possible, but
avoid having numerous links when writing for beginners to avoid distractions.

docs.title: Packaging Marmotta
docs.markdown:
# Packaging Marmotta

This directory contains the package-manager recipes for Marmotta. They are rendered from the
release executables and the `SHA256SUMS` asset that the `Release binaries` workflow publishes.

## Generated output

`node scripts/packages.mjs` writes to `packaging/out/` (git-ignored):

```text
packaging/out/
├── artifacts/                 # .deb, .rpm, .apk, and .pkg.tar.zst packages (with --build)
├── nfpm/                      # nfpm configs used to build the native packages
├── recipes/
│   ├── homebrew/marmotta.rb
│   ├── aur/PKGBUILD
│   ├── rpm/marmotta.spec
│   ├── alpine/APKBUILD
│   ├── nix/default.nix
│   ├── scoop/marmotta.json
│   └── winget/
└── manifest.json
```

## Generating recipes

Download the assets of a release and render everything:

```sh
gh release download v0.10.0 --dir dist
node scripts/packages.mjs --version 0.10.0 --sums dist/SHA256SUMS --artifacts dist --out packaging/out
```

To compute the checksums from binaries that are already on disk instead of using `SHA256SUMS`:

```sh
node scripts/packages.mjs --artifacts dist --out packaging/out
```

## Building native Linux packages

The `.deb`, `.rpm`, `.apk`, and Arch Linux packages are built with
[nfpm](https://nfpm.goreleaser.com/):

```sh
# https://github.com/goreleaser/nfpm/releases
node scripts/packages.mjs --artifacts dist --out packaging/out --build
```

The script verifies every package after building it: metadata (name, version, architecture) and
the installed files are read back from each package. Verification needs `tar` and `ar`; it uses
`rpm` or `bsdtar` to list RPM contents, and `bsdtar` (or `tar` with zstd support) for Arch Linux
packages. When `--sums` and `--build` are combined, the executables in `--artifacts` are checked
against `SHA256SUMS` before any package is built, so a stale `dist/` cannot produce packages that
disagree with the published checksums.

Only plain `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` versions are supported: nfpm rewrites pre-release and build
metadata differently per package format, which would make the generated spec and APKBUILD invalid.

The recipes reference `LICENSE` at tag `v<version>`. When that tag exists locally, the renderer
hashes the committed blob from the tag (`git show v<version>:LICENSE`); otherwise it uses the
working tree, so render an older version from a checkout of that tag. The Alpine recipe also needs
the release executables in `--artifacts` to compute the SHA-512 checksums that aports requires.

The `.apk` packages built by nfpm are unsigned. Add `--allow-untrusted` when installing them
directly, or sign them for a repository.

The release workflow installs a pinned nfpm version through
`.github/actions/setup-packaging`, runs `node --test test/packaging.test.js` with that nfpm, and
attaches the results to the GitHub release together with `SHA256SUMS.packages` and
`marmotta-vX.Y.Z-packaging.tar.gz` (the rendered recipes and their manifest). Packaging runs in a
separate job after the binary release, so a packaging failure never blocks the executables.

A second CI job renders the recipes from fixture checksums and runs each one through its consumer:
`ruby -c` for the formula, `abuild validate` for the APKBUILD, `makepkg --printsrcinfo` for the
PKGBUILD, `rpmspec -P` and `rpmspec -q` for the spec, and `nix-instantiate --parse` for the Nix
expression. This catches recipe syntax that filling in the placeholders alone would not.

## Package-manager notes

| Manager | Recipe | Runtime notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Homebrew | `homebrew/marmotta.rb` | Installs the standalone binary from the release; no Node.js or npm required. macOS binaries are ad-hoc signed and not notarized. |
| AUR | `aur/PKGBUILD` | `marmotta-bin`, `x86_64` and `aarch64`, glibc binaries. Depends on `glibc`. |
| Arch Linux | built by nfpm | Same binary and dependencies as the AUR package. |
| Debian/Ubuntu | built by nfpm | Depends on `libc6`; the binary is the glibc build. |
| Fedora/RHEL | built by nfpm | Depends on `glibc`; `rpm/marmotta.spec` is provided for dist-git submissions. |
| Alpine | built by nfpm, `alpine/APKBUILD` | Uses the musl binaries and depends on `libstdc++` and `libgcc`. The single APKBUILD covers `x86_64` and `aarch64`, selects the source with a `$CARCH` case, and uses `sha512sums` as aports expects. The nfpm-built `.apk` files are unsigned, so install them with `apk add --allow-untrusted` unless you sign them for a repository. |
| Nix | `nix/default.nix` | Fetches the standalone binary for the current system from the release. On Linux, `autoPatchelfHook` rewrites the interpreter for NixOS and stripping is disabled so the Bun payload stays intact. |
| Scoop | `scoop/marmotta.json` | Windows x64 and ARM64 executables. |
| winget | `winget/*.yaml` | Portable installer for Windows x64 and ARM64. |

All packages install a `marmotta` executable. Zig is downloaded on first use unless a compatible
Zig is already on `PATH`, `MARMOTTA_ZIG_DIR` is set, or a release pins `zigVersion`. Package
maintainers may want to add Zig as an optional/recommended dependency so first use works offline.

## Publishing checklist

Packages are attached to every GitHub release so users can install them directly. Publishing to
the package-manager repositories themselves still happens from those repositories:

1. **Homebrew**: copy `homebrew/marmotta.rb` into the `napi-bindings/homebrew-tap` repository (or
   submit it to `homebrew-core`), update the tap, and run `brew audit --strict`.
2. **AUR**: push `aur/PKGBUILD` to the `marmotta-bin` AUR repository and run
   `makepkg --printsrcinfo > .SRCINFO` before committing.
3. **Debian/Ubuntu**: upload the `.deb` files to an APT repository with `dpkg-scanpackages`, or
   submit the package to Debian/Ubuntu. Generate `Packages`/`Release` metadata for the repository.
4. **Fedora/RHEL**: submit `rpm/marmotta.spec` through dist-git or build it in COPR. Upload the
   source asset to the lookaside cache.
5. **Alpine**: submit `alpine/APKBUILD` to `alpinelinux/aports` (or build it with `abuild`).
6. **Nixpkgs**: add `nix/default.nix` to `pkgs/by-name/ma/marmotta/package.nix`, or expose it as a
   flake/overlay first.
7. **Scoop**: copy `scoop/marmotta.json` to a Scoop bucket.
8. **winget**: submit the three files under `winget/` to `microsoft/winget-pkgs` with
   `wingetcreate submit`.

The recipes are version-specific, so regenerate them from the new `SHA256SUMS` for every release.
The release workflow does this automatically and uploads `marmotta-vX.Y.Z-packaging.tar.gz`.

docs.title: Marmotta is an OPEN Open Source Project
docs.markdown: # Marmotta is an OPEN Open Source Project ## What? Individuals making significant and valuable contributions are given commit-access to the project to contribute as they see fit. This project is more like an open wiki than a standard guarded open source project. See our [informal contributing guide](./docs/contributing.md) for more details on contributing to this project. ### I want to be a collaborator! If you think you meet the above criteria and we have not invited you yet, we are sorry! Feel free to reach out to a [Lead Maintainer](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta#team) privately with a few links to your valuable contributions. Read the [GOVERNANCE](GOVERNANCE.md) to get more information. ## Rules There are a few basic ground rules for contributors: 1. **No `--force` pushes** on `main` or modifying the Git history in any way after a PR has been merged. 1. **Non-main branches** ought to be used for ongoing work. 1. **External API changes and significant modifications** ought to be subject to an **internal pull request** to solicit feedback from other contributors. 1. Internal pull requests to solicit feedback are *encouraged* for any other non-trivial contribution but are left to the discretion of the contributor. 1. Contributors should attempt to adhere to the prevailing code style. 1. At least two contributors, or one core member, must approve pull requests before merging. 1. All integrated CI services must be green before a pull request can be merged. 1. A lead maintainer must merge SemVer-major changes in this repository. 1. If it is not possible to reach a consensus in a pull request, the decision is left to the lead maintainer's team. 1. Pure-AI contributions with no human in the loop are not welcome. Pull requests ***MUST*** be opened by a human. Pull requests opened by bots not managed by the napi-bindings organization will result in the bot being banned from the organization. ## Releases Declaring formal releases remains the prerogative of the lead maintainers. Do not bump version numbers in pull requests. Bump the version with `npm version` rather than editing `package.json` by hand: its `version` lifecycle script updates the constant in `src/version.ts` and stages it, so the npm package and the standalone executables report the same version. (`npm test` also fails when the two drift.) Pushing a `v*` tag triggers the `Release binaries` workflow, which builds the standalone executables for all supported platforms with `bun build --compile`, runs `scripts/smoke.mjs` against each one, and attaches them together with `SHA256SUMS` and provenance attestations to the GitHub release of that tag. The tag must match the version in `package.json` or the workflow fails. Maintainers can also run the workflow manually from the Actions tab to test it before tagging; the binaries are then only uploaded as workflow artifacts. ## Changes to this arrangement This is an experiment and feedback is welcome! This document may also be subject to pull requests or changes by contributors where you believe you have something valuable to add or change. # napi-bindings Organization Structure The napi-bindings structure is detailed in the [GOVERNANCE](GOVERNANCE.md) document. ### Onboarding Collaborators Welcome to the team! We are happy to have you. Before you start, please complete the following tasks: 1. Set up 2 factor authentication for GitHub and NPM - [GitHub 2FA](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa) - [NPM 2FA](https://docs.npmjs.com/about-two-factor-authentication/) 2. Open a pull request to [`napi-bindings/marmotta:HEAD`](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/pulls) that adds your name, username, and email to the team in the [README.md](./README.md) and [package.json](./package.json) files. The member lists are sorted alphabetically by last name; make sure to add your name in the proper order.. 3. Optionally, the person can be added as an Open Collective member by the lead team. ### Offboarding Collaborators We are thankful to you and we are really glad to have worked with you. We'd be really happy to see you here again if you want to come back, but for now the person that did the onboarding must: 1. Ask the collaborator if they want to stay or not. 1. If the collaborator can't work with us anymore, they should: 1. Open a pull request to [`napi-bindings/marmotta:HEAD`](https://github.com/napi-bindings/marmotta/pulls) and move themselves to the *Past Collaborators* section. ----------------------------------------- ## Developer's Certificate of Origin 1.1 By making a contribution to this project, I certify that: * (a) The contribution was created in whole or in part by me and I have the right to submit it under the open source license indicated in the file; or * (b) The contribution is based upon previous work that, to the best of my knowledge, is covered under an appropriate open source license and I have the right under that license to submit that work with modifications, whether created in whole or in part by me, under the same open source license (unless I am permitted to submit under a different license), as indicated in the file; or * (c) The contribution was provided directly to me by some other person who certified (a), (b) or (c) and I have not modified it. * (d) I understand and agree that this project and the contribution are public and that a record of the contribution (including all personal information I submit with it, including my sign-off) is maintained indefinitely and may be redistributed consistent with this project or the open source license(s) involved.

docs.title: Marmotta Project Governance
docs.markdown:
# Marmotta Project Governance

<!-- TOC -->

* [Lead Maintainers](#lead-maintainers)
* [Collaborators](#collaborators)
  * [Collaborator activities](#collaborator-activities)
* [Great Contributors](#great-contributors)
* [Collaborator nominations](#collaborator-nominations)
* [Lead Maintainers nominations](#lead-maintainers-nominations)
* [Consensus seeking process](#consensus-seeking-process)

<!-- /TOC -->

## Lead Maintainers

Marmotta Lead Maintainers are the organization owners.
They are the only members of the `@napi-bindings/leads` team. The Lead
Maintainers are the curator of the Marmotta project and their key responsibility
is to issue releases of Marmotta and its dependencies.

## Collaborators

Marmotta Collaborators maintain the projects of the napi-bindings organization.

Collaborators have:

* Commit access to the projects repository
* Grant to release new versions of the project

Both Collaborators and non-Collaborators may propose changes to the source code
of the projects of the organization. The mechanism to propose such a change is a
GitHub pull request. Collaborators review and merge (_land_) pull requests
following the [CONTRIBUTING](CONTRIBUTING.md#rules) guidelines.

### Collaborator activities

* Helping users and novice contributors
* Contributing code and documentation changes that improve the project
* Reviewing and commenting on issues and pull requests
* Participation in working groups
* Merging pull requests
* Release plugins

After two years of inactivity, the Lead Maintainers can
remove inactive Collaborators or provide them with
_Past Collaborators_ status.
Past Collaborators may request that the Lead
Maintainers restore them to active status.


## Great Contributors

Great contributors on a specific area in the napi-bindings ecosystem will be invited
to join this group by Lead Maintainers. This group has the same permissions of a
contributor.

## Collaborator nominations

Individuals making significant and valuable contributions to the project may be
a candidate to join the napi-bindings organization.

A Collaborator needs to open a private team discussion on GitHub and list the
candidates they want to sponsor with a link to the user's contributions. For
example:

* Activities in the napi-bindings organization
  `[USERNAME](https://github.com/search?q=author:USERNAME+org:napi-bindings)`

Otherwise, a Contributor may self-apply if they believe they meet the above
criteria by reaching out to a Lead Maintainer privately with the links to their
valuable contributions. The Lead Maintainers will reply to the Contributor and
will decide whether the candidate should be made a Collaborator.

The consensus to grant a new candidate Collaborator status is reached when:

- at least one of the Lead Maintainers approve
- at least two of the Collaborators approve

After these conditions are satisfied, the [onboarding
process](CONTRIBUTING.md#onboarding-collaborators) may start.


## Lead Maintainers nominations

A Team Member may be promoted to a Lead Maintainers only through nomination by a
Lead maintainer and with agreement from the rest of Lead Maintainers.


## Consensus seeking process

The napi-bindings organization follows a [Consensus Seeking][] decision-making model.

[Consensus Seeking]:
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensus-seeking_decision-making

meta.description: A framework for building compiled Node.js add-ons in Go via Node-API

releases.name: napi-go v0.1.0
releases.body:
The first release: native Node.js addons written in Go, with the tooling of napi-rs.

### Framework (Layer 2, package `napi`)

- `napi.Export` of functions, classes and constants, with generic wrappers (`FuncN`, `FuncEN`,
  `ProcN`, `ProcEN`, `AsyncN`, `AsyncProcN`, `MethodN`, `CtorN`, …) for up to 8 parameters.
- Automatic conversions from the Go types: numbers (integers range-checked), strings, `[]byte`
  (views of JS memory), slices, arrays, maps, structs (`napi`/`json` tags), pointers, `any`,
  `*big.Int`, `time.Time`, `Either[A, B]`, napi values, and types implementing `FromJS`/`ToJS`.
  Conversion errors name the argument and the path inside it.
- Asynchronous functions: a `context.Context` first parameter runs the function in a goroutine and
  returns a Promise.
- Classes backed by Go values (`NewClass`), with methods, accessors, statics, `Finalize`, and the
  same JS object for the same `*T`.
- `JSFunc[A, R]`: goroutines call JS functions and receive the converted result.
- A C trampoline converts numbers, booleans and short strings and unwraps `this` with one cgo
  crossing per call; no Go allocation per call for primitives, Buffers, methods and accessors.

### Core (Layer 1, package `napi`)

- Typed JS values (`Value`, `Object`, `Function`, `String`, `BigInt`, `Buffer`, `TypedArray`, …),
  Go errors thrown as JS exceptions with kind and code, panics as `GO_PANIC`.
- Functions, classes (`DefineClass`), properties, references, finalizers, `Wrap`, type tags,
  externals, handle scopes, cleanup hooks, instance data per env, zero-copy and external buffers.
- Concurrency: `Env.Async` (Promises settled from goroutines), `ThreadsafeFunction[T]`,
  `Env.Context` (canceled when the env is destroyed), `Ref.DeleteLater`; one dispatcher per env
  wakes the JS thread once for a batch of results.
- Worker threads: the addon loads in every env, with separate state.

### Node-API bindings (Layer 0, package `sys`)

- The 154 functions of Node-API 1–10, generated 1:1, resolved at run time from the Node.js process
  (no import library, builds without Node.js).
- Declared Node-API version 8 by default, 9 and 10 with build tags.
- Coexistence of the Go runtime with Node.js signals: `SA_ONSTACK` added to the handlers Node.js
  installs later (Linux), `SA_RESETHAND` restored for SIGINT and SIGTERM (macOS), and a guard
  against a second Go runtime on macOS x64.

### Code generator (`napi-go gen`)

- `//napi:export`, `//napi:class`, `//napi:constructor`, `//napi:getter`, `//napi:setter`,
  `//napi:skip`, `//napi:object`, `//napi:type`, `//napi:returns`.
- Generates the registrations (`zz_napi.go`), `index.d.ts` with the Go comments as JSDoc, and
  `index.js`; reports unsupported types with file and line; `-check` for CI.

### CLI (`cmd/napi-go`)

- `napi-go new`: a project with an annotated example, tests and a GitHub Actions workflow that
  builds, tests and publishes every target.
- `napi-go build`: targets `linux-x64-gnu`, `linux-arm64-gnu`, `darwin-x64`, `darwin-arm64`,
  `win32-x64-gnu`, `win32-arm64-gnu`; cross-compilation from any host with zig (Linux binaries for
  glibc 2.17); format check of each binary.
- `napi-go artifacts` and `napi-go prepublish`: one npm package per platform and
  `optionalDependencies`, as napi-rs; `index.js` loads the binary of the running platform.

### Known limitations

- musl (Alpine Linux) is not supported by any Go release (golang/go#71953).
- macOS x64: one Go addon per process (golang/go#23617).
- A call into Go costs about 100 ns on Linux and about 1 µs on Windows; see `bench/README.md`.
- Intermittent failure, under investigation, of one end-to-end signal test on Linux arm64 CI
  runners (a hang or a SIGBUS while the test floods every thread with signals).

[0.1.0]: https://github.com/napi-bindings/napi-go/releases/tag/v0.1.0

projects.readme:
# napi-go

Native Node.js addons (`.node`) written in Go, on top of
[Node-API](https://nodejs.org/api/n-api.html): annotated Go functions, structs and classes become
a typed npm package, built for every platform from one machine. The design follows
[napi-rs](https://napi.rs).

```go
// Greet returns a greeting for name.
//
//napi:export
func Greet(name string) string { return "hello " + name }

// Download fetches url in a goroutine; JS gets a Promise.
//
//napi:export
func Download(ctx context.Context, url string) ([]byte, error) { … }
```

```ts
import { greet, download } from 'my-addon'   // typed by the generated index.d.ts
greet('Ann')
const body = await download('https://example.com')   // a Buffer
```

```sh
go run github.com/napi-bindings/napi-go/cmd/napi-go@latest new my-addon
cd my-addon && npm run build:debug && npm test
```

- **Conversions from Go types**: numbers, strings, `[]byte`, slices, maps, structs, pointers,
  `*big.Int`, `time.Time`; wrong JS arguments throw a TypeError naming the argument.
- **Goroutines**: functions with a `context.Context` return Promises; goroutines call JS functions
  with `JSFunc`; Promises settled in bulk cost one wake-up of the JS thread.
- **Classes** backed by Go values, with methods, getters, setters and finalizers.
- **TypeScript declarations** generated from the Go code, Go comments as JSDoc.
- **One machine builds all platforms**: Linux, macOS and Windows on x64 and arm64, with zig;
  one npm package per platform, as napi-rs.
- **Worker threads**, Node-API 8 to 10, and the Node.js and node-addon-api test suites ported to
  napi-go.

> **Status:** 0.1, the first release ([CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md)). Before 1.0 the API may change
> between minor versions.

## Documentation

| | |
|---|---|
| [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) | create, build, test and publish an addon |
| [Writing addons](docs/guide.md) | functions, types, errors, async, classes, calling JS |
| [How it works](docs/architecture.md) | layers, threads, memory, signals, costs |
| [Coming from napi-rs](docs/napi-rs.md) | the napi-rs features in napi-go |
| [Platforms and limitations](docs/platforms.md) | support, known limits, troubleshooting |
| [Benchmarks](bench/README.md) | against napi-rs and node-addon-api |
| [API reference](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/napi-bindings/napi-go/napi) | pkg.go.dev |

## Platforms

Linux (glibc) x64 and arm64, macOS arm64 and x64, Windows x64 and arm64, with Go 1.24 or later and
Node.js 22 or later. Not supported: musl (Alpine), which no Go release can load as a shared
library. On macOS x64, one Go addon per process. See [platforms](docs/platforms.md).

## Repository

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| [`napi/`](napi/README.md) | Layer 2 (framework: `Export`, wrappers, conversions, classes) and Layer 1 (core: values, errors, functions, buffers, threads) |
| [`sys/`](sys/README.md) | Layer 0: the Node-API 1–10 functions, generated 1:1 |
| [`cmd/napi-go/`](cmd/napi-go/README.md) | the CLI: `new`, `gen`, `build`, `artifacts`, `prepublish` |
| [`internal/codegen/`](internal/codegen/README.md) | the code generator: annotations and TypeScript mapping |
| [`bench/`](bench/README.md) | benchmarks |
| `tests/e2e/` | test addons and `node:test` suites |
| [`tests/nodesuite/`](tests/nodesuite/README.md), [`tests/addonapisuite/`](tests/addonapisuite/README.md) | the Node.js and node-addon-api test suites, ported |
| `.github/workflows/` | CI: `sys.yml` (layers, generator, CLI tests, Alpine sentinel), `cli.yml` (projects created by the CLI, cross-compiled and loaded on every platform), `bench.yml`, `release.yml` |

Developing napi-go itself:

```bash
go test ./sys/... ./napi/... ./internal/... ./cmd/...
node tests/e2e/build.mjs               # Windows without gcc: set CC=zig cc
node --test tests/e2e/*.test.mjs
node tests/nodesuite/run.mjs          # Node.js test suite ported to sys
node tests/addonapisuite/run.mjs      # node-addon-api test suite ported to napi
```

Releases: [docs/releasing.md](docs/releasing.md). License: [Apache 2.0](LICENSE).
projects.changelog:
# Changelog

All notable changes to napi-go. The format follows [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/),
and versions follow [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/): before 1.0.0, a minor version may
change the API (the changes are listed here).

## [0.1.0] - 2026-11-12

The first release: native Node.js addons written in Go, with the tooling of napi-rs.

### Framework (Layer 2, package `napi`)

- `napi.Export` of functions, classes and constants, with generic wrappers (`FuncN`, `FuncEN`,
  `ProcN`, `ProcEN`, `AsyncN`, `AsyncProcN`, `MethodN`, `CtorN`, …) for up to 8 parameters.
- Automatic conversions from the Go types: numbers (integers range-checked), strings, `[]byte`
  (views of JS memory), slices, arrays, maps, structs (`napi`/`json` tags), pointers, `any`,
  `*big.Int`, `time.Time`, `Either[A, B]`, napi values, and types implementing `FromJS`/`ToJS`.
  Conversion errors name the argument and the path inside it.
- Asynchronous functions: a `context.Context` first parameter runs the function in a goroutine and
  returns a Promise.
- Classes backed by Go values (`NewClass`), with methods, accessors, statics, `Finalize`, and the
  same JS object for the same `*T`.
- `JSFunc[A, R]`: goroutines call JS functions and receive the converted result.
- A C trampoline converts numbers, booleans and short strings and unwraps `this` with one cgo
  crossing per call; no Go allocation per call for primitives, Buffers, methods and accessors.

### Core (Layer 1, package `napi`)

- Typed JS values (`Value`, `Object`, `Function`, `String`, `BigInt`, `Buffer`, `TypedArray`, …),
  Go errors thrown as JS exceptions with kind and code, panics as `GO_PANIC`.
- Functions, classes (`DefineClass`), properties, references, finalizers, `Wrap`, type tags,
  externals, handle scopes, cleanup hooks, instance data per env, zero-copy and external buffers.
- Concurrency: `Env.Async` (Promises settled from goroutines), `ThreadsafeFunction[T]`,
  `Env.Context` (canceled when the env is destroyed), `Ref.DeleteLater`; one dispatcher per env
  wakes the JS thread once for a batch of results.
- Worker threads: the addon loads in every env, with separate state.

### Node-API bindings (Layer 0, package `sys`)

- The 154 functions of Node-API 1–10, generated 1:1, resolved at run time from the Node.js process
  (no import library, builds without Node.js).
- Declared Node-API version 8 by default, 9 and 10 with build tags.
- Coexistence of the Go runtime with Node.js signals: `SA_ONSTACK` added to the handlers Node.js
  installs later (Linux), `SA_RESETHAND` restored for SIGINT and SIGTERM (macOS), and a guard
  against a second Go runtime on macOS x64.

### Code generator (`napi-go gen`)

- `//napi:export`, `//napi:class`, `//napi:constructor`, `//napi:getter`, `//napi:setter`,
  `//napi:skip`, `//napi:object`, `//napi:type`, `//napi:returns`.
- Generates the registrations (`zz_napi.go`), `index.d.ts` with the Go comments as JSDoc, and
  `index.js`; reports unsupported types with file and line; `-check` for CI.

### CLI (`cmd/napi-go`)

- `napi-go new`: a project with an annotated example, tests and a GitHub Actions workflow that
  builds, tests and publishes every target.
- `napi-go build`: targets `linux-x64-gnu`, `linux-arm64-gnu`, `darwin-x64`, `darwin-arm64`,
  `win32-x64-gnu`, `win32-arm64-gnu`; cross-compilation from any host with zig (Linux binaries for
  glibc 2.17); format check of each binary.
- `napi-go artifacts` and `napi-go prepublish`: one npm package per platform and
  `optionalDependencies`, as napi-rs; `index.js` loads the binary of the running platform.

### Known limitations

- musl (Alpine Linux) is not supported by any Go release (golang/go#71953).
- macOS x64: one Go addon per process (golang/go#23617).
- A call into Go costs about 100 ns on Linux and about 1 µs on Windows; see `bench/README.md`.
- Intermittent failure, under investigation, of one end-to-end signal test on Linux arm64 CI
  runners (a hang or a SIGBUS while the test floods every thread with signals).

[0.1.0]: https://github.com/napi-bindings/napi-go/releases/tag/v0.1.0

docs.title: How it works
docs.markdown:
# How it works

## Layers

```
 your addon     //napi: annotations ──napi-go gen──▶ zz_napi.go, index.js, index.d.ts
      │
 Layer 2        napi.Export, FuncN/AsyncN/MethodN, NewClass, codecs (Go ⇄ JS conversions), JSFunc
 Layer 1        napi.Env, Value, Object, Function, errors, Ref, Async, ThreadsafeFunction
 Layer 0        sys: the Node-API C functions 1:1, C trampolines, symbol loader
      │
 Node.js        Node-API (napi_*), V8, libuv
```

Each layer only uses the one below. Layer 2 and Layer 1 are both in package `napi` and can be
mixed in one addon; Layer 0 (`sys`) is for raw ABI access.

## Loading

The addon is a shared library built by `go build -buildmode=c-shared`, renamed `.node`. When
`require()` loads it:

1. The dynamic loader runs the Go runtime initialization (the runtime starts its threads, the
   `init` functions run and register the exports).
2. Node.js calls the entry point `napi_register_module_v1` (`sys/module.c`), which resolves every
   Node-API function from the host process with `dlsym` or `GetProcAddress`. The library has no
   undefined symbols and no import library: it builds without Node.js installed, and a function
   missing from the running Node.js is reported, not a crash at load time.
3. For every env that loads the addon (the main thread, each worker thread), the registered exports
   are created.

The declared Node-API version is 8 by default, 9 or 10 with the build tags `napi_go_v9` and
`napi_go_v10` ([sys](../sys/README.md#declared-node-api-version)).

## A call

```
JS add(1, 2)
 └▶ V8 ─▶ Node-API ─▶ C trampoline (sys/typed.c): reads 1 and 2 as doubles
                       └▶ one cgo callback into Go: the Go function, by its ID in a table
                       ◀─ result 3 as a double
                      C creates the JS number
```

- **One crossing per call.** Numbers, booleans and strings up to about 500 bytes are converted in
  C, before and after the single crossing into Go, as is the `this` of methods. Other types are
  converted in Go by codecs: one per Go type, built once with reflection and cached, working on
  `unsafe` pointers at run time, with no Go allocation for primitives, `[]byte`, napi values and
  class pointers.
- **The crossing is the floor.** Node.js calls on its own thread, which is not a Go thread; entering
  Go costs about 100 ns on Linux (about 1 µs on Windows, where the Go runtime lacks an
  optimization for threads created outside Go). A call from Rust or C++ costs a few nanoseconds.
  The [benchmarks](../bench/README.md) compare the three.
- **Errors** returned by Go are thrown as JS exceptions on the way out; panics are recovered and
  thrown as `GO_PANIC`.

## Threads

V8 runs JavaScript on one thread per env, and every Node-API call must be made on it. Goroutines
run on the threads of the Go scheduler, so they never call Node-API: they hand work to the JS
thread.

- **One dispatcher per env.** Each env has one threadsafe function (unref'd: it does not keep
  Node.js alive) and a Go queue of closures. A goroutine appends to the queue, and wakes the JS
  thread only if the queue was empty: a thousand goroutines finishing together cost one wake-up.
- **Async functions** (`AsyncN`, `Env.Async`) convert the arguments on the JS thread, run the Go
  function in a goroutine, and settle the Promise through the dispatcher. Node.js stays alive while
  any is pending.
- **ThreadsafeFunction[T]** and **JSFunc[A, R]** let goroutines call JS functions (with the result
  converted back, for `JSFunc`).
- **Env context.** `Env.Context()` is canceled when the env is destroyed (worker terminated,
  process exiting); pending Promises are dropped and threadsafe functions return `ErrClosing`.

## Memory

Two garbage collectors manage the objects of an addon: V8 for JS values, Go for Go values. cgo
forbids handing Go pointers to C for C to keep, so:

- **Go values given to JS are found by ID.** Callbacks, class instances, externals and finalizers
  live in Go tables; Node-API receives an integer. When V8 collects the JS object, its finalizer
  frees the ID and the Go value becomes collectable. Reads of the tables are lock-free.
- **JS values held by Go are references** (`Value.NewRef`, napi_ref), released explicitly or from
  a goroutine with `Ref.DeleteLater`. A plain `napi.Value` is valid only during the call.
- **Buffers.** A `[]byte` parameter is a view of V8 memory, valid during the call. A returned
  `[]byte` is copied into a new Buffer. `NewExternalBuffer` hands Go memory to JS without a copy,
  pinned with `runtime.Pinner` until V8 releases it.
- **Class instances.** A JS instance holds the ID of its `*T`. In an env, the same `*T` always maps
  to the same JS object, and `Finalize` runs when the last instance is collected.

## Signals

The Go runtime and Node.js both install signal handlers in one process. Go requires every handler
to run on the alternate signal stack (`SA_ONSTACK`): a signal can arrive on a Go thread, whose
stack is small. Handlers that Node.js and libuv install after the addon has loaded
(`process.on('SIGINT')`, child processes) lack the flag; on Linux, `sys/onstack.c` adds it to
them by intercepting `sigaction` in the process. On macOS, the Go runtime reinstalls the handlers
that are already there to add `SA_ONSTACK`, and the macOS kernel does not report `SA_RESETHAND`,
so the flag is lost on the handler that Node.js uses to exit on SIGINT and SIGTERM; the handler
then calls itself forever. `sys/sigfix.c` restores the flag. The e2e
tests check WebAssembly traps, child processes, SIGINT and SIGTERM with the addon loaded and Go
busy.

## Source map

| Path | |
|---|---|
| `sys/` | Layer 0: generated bindings, loader, trampolines, signal fixes |
| `napi/` | Layers 1 and 2 |
| `internal/codegen/` | the generator of `napi-go gen` |
| `sys/internal/gen/`, `napi/internal/genwrappers/` | generators of `sys` and of the Layer 2 wrappers |
| `cmd/napi-go/` | the CLI |
| `tests/` | e2e addons and tests, the Node.js and node-addon-api test suites ported to napi-go |
| `bench/` | benchmarks |

docs.title: Getting started
docs.markdown:
# Getting started

## Requirements

- **Go 1.24** or later, with cgo.
- **A C compiler**: gcc or clang on Linux and macOS; on Windows MinGW gcc, or
  [zig](https://ziglang.org/download/) (`napi-go build -zig always`).
- **Node.js 22** or later.
- Optional: **zig**, to build for other platforms (`napi-go build -target …`) and to make Linux
  release binaries that run on older distributions (glibc 2.17).

## Create a project

```sh
go run github.com/napi-bindings/napi-go/cmd/napi-go@latest new my-addon
cd my-addon
npm run build:debug
npm test
```

`napi-go new` creates:

| File | |
|---|---|
| `main.go` | the addon: annotated Go functions and a class |
| `go.mod` | requires napi-go as a library and as a tool, so `go tool napi-go` runs the CLI at the version of the library |
| `package.json` | the npm package; `napiGo` holds the napi-go configuration |
| `test/index.test.mjs` | tests with `node:test` |
| `.github/workflows/CI.yml` | builds and tests every target, publishes on a version tag |
| `.gitignore`, `README.md` | |

`npm run build:debug` runs `go tool napi-go build`, which first generates `zz_napi.go`,
`index.js` and `index.d.ts` from the annotations, then builds `my-addon.<target>.node` for this
machine. Commit the generated files: they are part of the package.

## Write a function

```go
// Greet returns a greeting for name.
//
//napi:export
func Greet(name string) string { return "hello " + name }
```

```sh
npm run build:debug
node -e "console.log(require('.').greet('Ann'))"
```

From TypeScript and ES modules the exports have types and names:

```ts
import { greet } from 'my-addon'
greet('Ann')   // greet(name: string): string, with the Go comment as JSDoc
```

The [guide](guide.md) covers the parameter and result types, errors, async functions and classes.

## Build for other platforms

```sh
go tool napi-go build -release                        # this machine
go tool napi-go build -release -target linux-arm64-gnu
go tool napi-go build -release -target all            # the targets of package.json
```

Builds for another platform use zig as C compiler. The targets are `linux-x64-gnu`,
`linux-arm64-gnu`, `darwin-x64`, `darwin-arm64`, `win32-x64-gnu` and `win32-arm64-gnu`; see the
[CLI reference](../cmd/napi-go/README.md#targets).

## Publish

The package follows the layout of napi-rs: the main package holds `index.js` and `index.d.ts`, and
each target has a package `my-addon-<target>` with its `.node` file, installed by npm only on
matching machines.

The workflow created by `new` does it all: push a tag `v<version>` equal to the version of
`package.json`, with the repository secret `NPM_TOKEN`. By hand:

```sh
go tool napi-go artifacts -d <directory with the built .node files>
go tool napi-go prepublish -publish
npm publish
```

## Without the template

An existing Go module can become an addon without `napi-go new`:

```sh
go get github.com/napi-bindings/napi-go@latest
go get -tool github.com/napi-bindings/napi-go/cmd/napi-go
```

Write a `main` package with an empty `func main() {}` and annotated declarations, then
`go tool napi-go build` (without `package.json` the binary is named after the directory). Or skip
the generator and register with `napi.Export` in an `init` function
([`napi` package](../napi/README.md)), and build with
`go build -buildmode=c-shared -o addon.node .`.
