projects.readme:
# Node-API Stub

![Node-API Build Matrix](https://github.com/napi-bindings/node-api-stub/workflows/Node-API%20Build%20Matrix/badge.svg)

- [Introduction](#introduction)
- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [Using it from CMake](#using-it-from-cmake)
- [Targets and options](#targets-and-options)
- [Stub libraries](#stub-libraries)
- [Building and testing](#building-and-testing)
- [Updating the Node-API headers](#updating-the-node-api-headers)
- [Migrating from 8.x](#migrating-from-8x)
- [Code of conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)
- [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md)
- [Team](#the-team)
- [Acknowledgements](#acknowledgements)
- [License](#license)

## Introduction

A native addon for Node.js calls the Node-API functions (`napi_*`, `node_api_*`)
exported by the host process (`node`, `node.exe`, Electron, ...). When the addon
is built, those symbols do not exist yet, and some toolchains refuse to link:
Windows always needs an import library, macOS rejects undefined symbols by
default, and on Linux some build systems add `-z defs`.

This project gives CMake projects (and any other build system) everything they
need to link an addon on every platform, without Node.js installed:

- the official Node-API headers, vendored from
  [node-api-headers](https://github.com/nodejs/node-api-headers) (Node-API 10);
- a `NodeApi::NodeApi` target that applies the right link mechanism for the
  platform;
- optional static and shared stub libraries for the cases that need them.

## How it works

The addon must always end up calling the Node-API functions of the host
process. A library with function bodies linked into the addon can be called
instead of them, so the right mechanism depends on the platform:

| Platform | What `NodeApi::NodeApi` does |
|---|---|
| Windows, MSVC / clang-cl (x64, x86, arm64) | links `node_api.lib`, an import library for `NODE.EXE` generated from the official `.def` file, plus `/DELAYLOAD:node.exe` and a delay-load hook so that the addon also loads in hosts with another name (Electron, a renamed `node.exe`) |
| Windows, MinGW / llvm-mingw | links `libnode_api.dll.a`, generated with `dlltool` |
| macOS | `-Wl,-U,_<symbol>` for each Node-API symbol: only those may stay undefined (or `-undefined dynamic_lookup`, see options) |
| Linux, BSD, Android (ELF) | nothing is linked; adds `-z undefs` so that `-z defs` does not reject the Node-API symbols |

The import libraries are generated at configure time, so the project builds
from source anywhere a C compiler is available; prebuilt archives are also
attached to each release.

> **Why not a stub everywhere?** A stub linked into the addon is called instead
> of Node-API when the linker binds the calls inside the addon: always on
> Windows and macOS, and on Linux when the addon is linked with `-Bsymbolic`.
> `go build -buildmode=c-shared` always passes `-Bsymbolic`, so a Go addon
> linked with the static stub calls the empty functions. The tests in
> [`tests/`](tests/CMakeLists.txt) reproduce this case.

## Using it from CMake

```cmake
# A) from source (recommended)
include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(node_api_stub
  GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/napi-bindings/node-api-stub.git
  GIT_TAG        v10.0.0)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(node_api_stub)

# B) from an installed package or a release archive
# find_package(NodeApi 10 REQUIRED CONFIG)

add_library(my_addon MODULE addon.c)
set_target_properties(my_addon PROPERTIES PREFIX "" SUFFIX ".node")
target_link_libraries(my_addon PRIVATE NodeApi::NodeApi)
```

`add_subdirectory(node-api-stub)` works the same way as `FetchContent`.

## Targets and options

| Target | Content |
|---|---|
| `NodeApi::NodeApi` | **use this one.** Headers, `NAPI_VERSION`, `BUILDING_NODE_EXTENSION` and the platform link mechanism |
| `NodeApi::headers` | headers and compile definitions only |
| `NodeApi::stub` | static stub, position-independent |
| `NodeApi::stub_shared` | shared stub |
| `NodeApi::legacy` | alias of `NodeApi::stub`, for projects that used the old `node_api` target |

| Option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `NODE_API_VERSION` | `8` | `NAPI_VERSION` defined for consumers; `experimental` defines `NAPI_EXPERIMENTAL`; empty to leave it to the consumer |
| `NODE_API_BUILD_STUB_STATIC` | ON on ELF, OFF on Windows/macOS | build `NodeApi::stub` |
| `NODE_API_BUILD_STUB_SHARED` | ON on ELF, OFF on Windows/macOS | build `NodeApi::stub_shared` |
| `NODE_API_ELF_ALLOW_UNDEFINED` | ON | add `-z undefs` on ELF |
| `NODE_API_MACOS_UNDEFINED` | `symbols` | `symbols` (`-U` per Node-API symbol) or `dynamic_lookup` |
| `NODE_API_WIN_DELAY_LOAD` | ON | MSVC: delay-load `node.exe` and redirect it to the host executable |
| `NODE_API_INSTALL` | ON when top level | install and export rules |
| `NODE_API_BUILD_TESTS` | ON when top level | tests that load the addons in Node.js |

When the project is used as a dependency, the stub libraries are excluded from
`all` and are built only if a target links them.

## Stub libraries

The stubs are generated from `def/node_api.def`: each function prints its own
name and calls `abort()`. They must never run; if they do, the addon fails
loudly instead of carrying on with uninitialised values.

- **Static (`libnode_api_stub.a`)**: for toolchains that need an archive to
  link and do not accept linker options. On ELF it works only through symbol
  interposition: do not use it with `-Bsymbolic`, and therefore not with Go
  `-buildmode=c-shared`.
- **Shared (`libnode_api_stub.so`)**: correct even with `-Bsymbolic`, but the
  addon records a `DT_NEEDED` entry for it: remove it after linking
  (`patchelf --remove-needed libnode_api_stub.so addon.node`) or ship the
  library next to the addon.
- **Windows and macOS**: not recommended; built only on explicit request.

Other options that avoid the link problem entirely are resolving the Node-API
functions at run time (`dlsym(RTLD_DEFAULT, ...)` / `GetProcAddress`), as
[napi-rs](https://napi.rs) does, or declaring them as weak references on ELF
(`#pragma weak napi_create_object`).

## Building and testing

You need CMake 3.16 or later and a C compiler. Node.js is optional and is used
only by the tests, which load the test addons and check that their calls reach
the real Node-API.

```
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --config Release
ctest --test-dir build -C Release --output-on-failure
cmake --install build --config Release --prefix ./dist
```

On Windows use the Visual Studio generator (`-A x64`, `-A Win32`, `-A ARM64`)
or MinGW / llvm-mingw with `-G Ninja`.

## Updating the Node-API headers

`include/` and `def/` come unmodified from the
[node-api-headers](https://www.npmjs.com/package/node-api-headers) npm package.
To update them (Node.js and npm are not needed):

```
cmake -DVERSION=1.9.0 -P scripts/update-node-api-headers.cmake
```

## Migrating from 8.x

- The headers moved from the repository root to `include/`; `node_api.c` is
  now generated.
- Replace the `node_api` target with `NodeApi::NodeApi`. If you really need the
  old static archive, link `NodeApi::legacy` (on ELF only).
- The static library is now called `libnode_api_stub.a`, and its functions
  abort instead of returning `napi_ok`.

## The Team

### Nicola Del Gobbo

<https://github.com/NickNaso/>

<https://www.npmjs.com/~nicknaso>

<https://twitter.com/NickNaso>

## Acknowledgements

Thank you to all people that encourage me every day.

## License

Licensed under [Apache license V2](./LICENSE).

The files in `include/` and `def/` come from
[node-api-headers](https://github.com/nodejs/node-api-headers) and are
licensed under the MIT license (see `def/LICENSE-node-api-headers`).

releases.name: Release 7.0.0
releases.body:
### Notable changes

* Update QuickJS to version 2026-06-04. The engine now supports most of ES2025:
  top-level await, WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry, iterator helpers, the Set
  methods, resizable ArrayBuffer, the RegExp `v` flag and modifiers,
  Float16Array, JSON modules with import attributes, `Promise.try`,
  `Math.sumPrecise` and more.
* The release archives are cross-compiled with `zig cc` from one Linux runner:
  13 native platforms instead of 5, plus WebAssembly (`wasm32-wasi` and
  `wasm32-emscripten`, engine only).
* New `qjs-windows-x86_64-mingw.zip` and `qjs-windows-x86-mingw.zip` archives,
  built natively on Windows with MinGW-w64 11 (MinGW-Builds GCC 13.2, msvcrt):
  they link with MinGW-w64 toolchains that cannot link the zig archives,
  including releases older than 12.
* The Linux archives no longer depend on the Ubuntu version of the CI runner:
  they need glibc 2.17 or later (2.27 for RISC-V). Static musl builds are also
  provided.
* New CMake options `QJS_BUILD_LIBC`, `QJS_BUILD_TOOLS`, `QJS_BUILD_SMOKE_TEST`
  and `QJSC_EXECUTABLE`; new `check` target that runs the QuickJS tests.
* New CMake toolchain file `toolchains/zig.cmake` and build script
  `scripts/build.sh`. `toolchains/linux_aarch64.cmake` and the dependency on
  qemu to build for arm64 were removed.
* The CI runs the tests on Linux x86_64, x86, arm64, armv7 and riscv64 and on
  real Windows and macOS runners, and publishes a `SHA256SUMS` file with every
  release.

### Breaking changes

#### QuickJS API

* The mathematical extensions were removed upstream: `CONFIG_BIGNUM`,
  `libbf`, `qjscalc`, BigFloat, BigDecimal and operator overloading are gone,
  together with `JS_AddIntrinsicBigFloat`, `JS_AddIntrinsicBigDecimal`,
  `JS_AddIntrinsicOperators`, `JS_EnableBignumExt`, `JS_IsBigFloat` and
  `JS_IsBigDecimal`. BigInt is always available and `JS_AddIntrinsicBigInt`
  no longer exists.
* `JS_EVAL_FLAG_STRIP` was removed: use `JS_SetStripInfo`.
* `JS_ResetUncatchableError` was removed: use `JS_SetUncatchableException`.
* `JS_RunModule` was removed: use `JS_LoadModule`.
* `JS_PROP_NO_ADD`, `JS_VALUE_GET_OBJ` and `JS_VALUE_GET_STRING` were removed
  from `quickjs.h`.
* `JS_SetPropertyInternal` has an additional `this_obj` parameter.
* `js_module_loader` (`quickjs-libc.h`) has an additional
  `JSValueConst attributes` parameter.
* The `JS_AddIntrinsic*` functions, `JS_SetConstructor` and
  `JS_SetPropertyFunctionList` now return `int` instead of `void`.

#### Archives

* The archives were renamed:

  | 6.0.0 | 7.0.0 |
  | --- | --- |
  | `qjs-windows.zip` | `qjs-windows-x86_64.zip` |
  | `qjs-ubuntu-18_04.zip`, `qjs-ubuntu-20_04.zip` | `qjs-linux-x86_64.zip` |
  | `qjs-linux-arm64.zip` | `qjs-linux-arm64.zip` |
  | `qjs-macOS.zip` | `qjs-macos-x86_64.zip`, `qjs-macos-arm64.zip` |

* The `qjs-windows-*.zip` archives are built with zig against the UCRT and a
  recent MinGW-w64. MinGW-w64 toolchains older than 12 cannot link them
  (undefined references to `pthread_cond_timedwait64` and `clock_gettime64`):
  use the `qjs-windows-*-mingw.zip` archives (msvcrt) instead.
* Every archive now contains `VERSION` and the QuickJS `LICENSE`.

#### Build

* CMake 3.20 or later is required.
* `CONFIG_BIGNUM` is no longer defined for the users of the `qjs` target.
* Cross-compiling the tools requires `-DQJSC_EXECUTABLE=<host qjsc>`.

projects.readme:
# QuickJS JavaScript Engine

[![QuickJS Build Matrix](https://github.com/napi-bindings/quickjs-build/actions/workflows/quickjs-build.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/napi-bindings/quickjs-build/actions/workflows/quickjs-build.yml)

## Version 2026-06-04

- [Introduction](#introduction)
- [Prebuilt archives](#prebuilt-archives)
- [Using the library](#using-the-library)
- [Using the WebAssembly builds](#using-the-webassembly-builds)
- [Building](#building)
- [Updating QuickJS](#updating-quickjs)
- [Code of conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)
- [References](#references)
- [Team](#team)
- [Acknowledgments](#acknowledgements)
- [License](#license)

## Introduction

**QuickJS** is a small and embeddable JavaScript engine. It supports most of the
**[ES2025](https://tc39.es/ecma262/)** specification including modules,
asynchronous generators, proxies and BigInt.

### Main Features:

- Small and easily embeddable: just a few **C** files, no external dependency,
**210 KiB** of x86 code for a simple hello world program.
- Fast interpreter with very low startup time: runs the tests of the
**[ECMAScript Test Suite](https://github.com/tc39/test262)** in less than 2
minutes on a single core of a desktop PC. The complete life cycle of a runtime
instance completes in less than 300 microseconds.
- Almost complete **ES2025** support.
- Passes nearly 100% of the
**[ECMAScript Test Suite](https://github.com/tc39/test262)** tests when selecting
the ES2025 features.
- Can compile JavaScript sources to executables with no external dependency.
- Garbage collection using reference counting (to reduce memory usage and have
deterministic behavior) with cycle removal.
- Command line interpreter with contextual colorization implemented in JavaScript.
- Small built-in standard library with **C** library wrappers.

This repository is a mirror of the original work that you can find
**[here](https://bellard.org/quickjs/)**. The files in `src/`, `include/` and
`tests/` are the unmodified files of the `quickjs-2026-06-04` release.

The mathematical extensions of the previous releases (BigFloat, BigDecimal,
operator overloading) were removed upstream and are no longer available. See the
[changelog](CHANGELOG.md) for the list of the API changes.

## Prebuilt archives

The main purpose of this repository is to build **QuickJS** as a static library
that you can include in your **C / C++** project. Every
[release](https://github.com/napi-bindings/quickjs-build/releases) provides the
following archives, together with a `SHA256SUMS` file:

| Archive | Platform | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `qjs-linux-x86_64.zip` | Linux x86_64 | glibc 2.17 or later |
| `qjs-linux-arm64.zip` | Linux AArch64 | glibc 2.17 or later |
| `qjs-linux-armv7.zip` | Linux ARMv7-A hard float | glibc 2.17 or later |
| `qjs-linux-riscv64.zip` | Linux RISC-V 64 (rv64gc) | glibc 2.27 or later |
| `qjs-linux-x86.zip` | Linux x86 32 bit | glibc 2.17 or later |
| `qjs-linux-x86_64-musl.zip` | Linux x86_64, musl | static executables, e.g. for Alpine |
| `qjs-linux-arm64-musl.zip` | Linux AArch64, musl | static executables, e.g. for Alpine |
| `qjs-windows-x86_64.zip` | Windows x86_64 | MinGW-w64 ABI, UCRT |
| `qjs-windows-arm64.zip` | Windows ARM64 | MinGW-w64 ABI, UCRT |
| `qjs-windows-x86.zip` | Windows x86 32 bit | MinGW-w64 ABI, UCRT |
| `qjs-windows-x86_64-mingw.zip` | Windows x86_64 | built with MinGW-w64 11 (GCC 13.2), msvcrt |
| `qjs-windows-x86-mingw.zip` | Windows x86 32 bit | built with MinGW-w64 11 (GCC 13.2), msvcrt |
| `qjs-macos-x86_64.zip` | macOS Intel | macOS 11 or later |
| `qjs-macos-arm64.zip` | macOS Apple Silicon | macOS 11 or later |
| `qjs-freebsd-x86_64.zip` | FreeBSD x86_64 | FreeBSD 14 or later |
| `qjs-wasm32-wasi.zip` | WebAssembly, WASI | engine only |
| `qjs-wasm32-emscripten.zip` | WebAssembly, Emscripten | engine only |

The native archives contain:

- `libqjs.a`: the static library (engine and `quickjs-libc`, the `std` and `os`
  modules);
- `qjsc`, `quickjs` and `run-test262`: the QuickJS compiler, the command line
  interpreter and the test262 runner;
- `include/`: `quickjs.h` and `quickjs-libc.h`;
- `VERSION` and `LICENSE`: the QuickJS version and its MIT license.

The WebAssembly archives contain `libqjs.a` with the engine only, `include/`,
`VERSION` and `LICENSE`.

The archives are cross-compiled from Linux with [`zig cc`](https://ziglang.org/)
at the version stored in [`.zigversion`](.zigversion), except
`qjs-wasm32-emscripten.zip` (Emscripten SDK) and the two `-mingw` archives, built
natively on Windows with the
[MinGW-Builds](https://github.com/niXman/mingw-builds-binaries) toolchain
`13.2.0-rt_v11-rev1`.

## Using the library

Compile and link your program against the content of the archive:

```
cc -Iinclude my_program.c libqjs.a -lm -lpthread -ldl -o my_program
```

`-ldl` is not needed on Windows, macOS and FreeBSD. On Windows add `-static` to
avoid the dependency on `libwinpthread-1.dll`.

[`smoke/embed.c`](smoke/embed.c) is a complete example that creates a runtime,
evaluates a script and reads the result back. The CI builds it for every target
and runs it wherever the binaries can be executed.

Notes for Windows:

- Two flavours of the Windows archives are provided. Pick the one that matches
  the toolchain you link with:

  | Your toolchain | Archive |
  | --- | --- |
  | MinGW-w64 12 or later with the UCRT: [MSYS2 UCRT64](https://www.msys2.org/docs/environments/), [llvm-mingw](https://github.com/mstorsjo/llvm-mingw), `zig cc` | `qjs-windows-x86_64.zip`, `qjs-windows-x86.zip`, `qjs-windows-arm64.zip` |
  | MinGW-w64 with the msvcrt runtime, including releases before 12: MSYS2 MINGW64, MinGW-Builds, Debian and Ubuntu `gcc-mingw-w64` | `qjs-windows-x86_64-mingw.zip`, `qjs-windows-x86-mingw.zip` |

- MinGW-w64 12 moved winpthreads to 64-bit `time_t` symbols: code compiled with
  its headers references `clock_gettime64` and `pthread_cond_timedwait64`, which
  older releases do not have. Linking the zig archives with an older MinGW-w64
  fails with undefined references to these two functions. The `-mingw` archives
  are compiled with MinGW-w64 11 and reference the classic names instead.
- Do not mix C runtimes: link the UCRT archives into UCRT programs and the
  `-mingw` (msvcrt) archives into msvcrt programs.
- Microsoft Visual C++ is not supported by QuickJS.

You can also add this repository to a **CMake** project and let it build the
library with your own toolchain:

```cmake
add_subdirectory(quickjs-build)
target_link_libraries(my_program PRIVATE qjs)
```

## Using the WebAssembly builds

Both WebAssembly archives contain the engine only: `quickjs-libc` needs
processes, pipes and signals that are not available there. Your program provides
what it needs (for example a `print` function) through the QuickJS C API.

### WASI

Link `libqjs.a` with a WASI toolchain such as `zig cc -target wasm32-wasi` or
[wasi-sdk](https://github.com/WebAssembly/wasi-sdk):

```
zig cc -target wasm32-wasi -O2 -Iinclude my_program.c libqjs.a \
  -Wl,-z,stack-size=1048576 -o my_program.wasm
```

The resulting module runs on any WASI runtime, for example
[Wasmtime](https://wasmtime.dev/) or Node.js (see
[`smoke/run-wasi.mjs`](smoke/run-wasi.mjs)).

**Set the stack limit of the runtime.** The WebAssembly call stack belongs to the
host and is invisible to the engine, which only measures the stack kept in the
linear memory. With the default limit of QuickJS (1 MiB) a runaway recursion
exhausts the call stack of the host first and the module traps instead of
throwing a JavaScript `InternalError`. Lower the limit right after creating the
runtime and give the module a linear memory stack larger than that limit:

```c
JSRuntime *rt = JS_NewRuntime();
JS_SetMaxStackSize(rt, 256 * 1024);
```

With these values the recursion test of `smoke/embed.c` ends with a catchable
exception on Node.js 22. Other hosts may need a different value.

### Emscripten

Link `libqjs.a` with `emcc`:

```
emcc -O2 -Iinclude my_program.c libqjs.a -o my_program.js
```

When built with Emscripten the engine disables `Atomics` and its own stack
check, so a runaway recursion ends with the `RangeError` of the host.

## Building

If you want to build the QuickJS library on your own the first step is to clone
this repository:

`> git clone https://github.com/napi-bindings/quickjs-build.git`

You need **CMake** 3.20 or later and **GCC** or **Clang**.

### Native build

```
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build
cmake --build build --target check
```

The last command runs the QuickJS tests stored in `tests/`.

On **Windows** install a MinGW-w64 toolchain (for example with
[MSYS2](https://www.msys2.org/)), be sure that `gcc` is in your path of execution
and add `-G "MinGW Makefiles"` to the first command.

On **Linux** install the dependencies with:

```
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install build-essential cmake -y
```

On **macOS** install the `Xcode Command Line Tools` running
`xcode-select --install` and CMake running `brew install cmake`.

`-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` could be set with one of the following two values:

- Release
- Debug

### Build options

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `QJS_BUILD_LIBC` | `ON`, `OFF` for WebAssembly | Include `quickjs-libc` (the `std` and `os` modules) in `libqjs.a` |
| `QJS_BUILD_TOOLS` | `ON`, `OFF` for WebAssembly | Build `qjsc`, `quickjs` and `run-test262` |
| `QJS_BUILD_SMOKE_TEST` | `OFF` | Build `smoke/embed.c` and add it to the tests |
| `QJSC_EXECUTABLE` | empty | `qjsc` built for the host, required to build the tools when cross-compiling |

### Cross-compiling with zig

[`toolchains/zig.cmake`](toolchains/zig.cmake) is a CMake toolchain file that
uses `zig cc` as the C compiler. With it one machine builds the library for all
the platforms of the table above, with no other cross-compiler or SDK. The CI
uses zig 0.17.1; the build also works with zig 0.16.0.

The script [`scripts/build.sh`](scripts/build.sh) runs the whole process and
writes the archives to `dist/`. It needs a POSIX shell (Linux, macOS, WSL):

```
sh scripts/build.sh --list
sh scripts/build.sh linux-arm64 windows-x86_64
sh scripts/build.sh --test linux-x86_64
sh scripts/build.sh all
```

The build has two stages, because the `quickjs` executable embeds the bytecode of
`repl.js` generated by `qjsc`, and a cross-compiled `qjsc` cannot run on the
build machine:

```
# 1. qjsc for the build machine
cmake -S . -B build/host -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build/host --target qjsc

# 2. the target
cmake -S . -B build/linux-arm64 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=toolchains/zig.cmake \
  -DZIG_TARGET=aarch64-linux-gnu.2.17 \
  -DQJSC_EXECUTABLE=$PWD/build/host/qjsc
cmake --build build/linux-arm64
```

`ZIG_TARGET` is a zig target triple; the suffix after the ABI selects the minimum
glibc version and the suffix after `macos` the minimum macOS version. Set
`CMAKE_CROSSCOMPILING_EMULATOR` to run the tests of a foreign architecture, for
example `-DCMAKE_CROSSCOMPILING_EMULATOR="qemu-aarch64;-L;/usr/aarch64-linux-gnu"`.

The WebAssembly targets have no tools and skip the first stage:

```
sh scripts/build.sh --test wasm32-wasi
sh scripts/build.sh --test wasm32-emscripten
```

The second command needs the [Emscripten SDK](https://emscripten.org/) with
`emcmake` in your path of execution, instead of zig.

## Updating QuickJS

The QuickJS files are copied without changes from the upstream tarball:

- `src/`: the `.c`, `.h` and `repl.js` files needed by the library and the tools;
- `include/`: `quickjs.h` and `quickjs-libc.h`;
- `tests/`: the test scripts run by the `check` target;
- `VERSION` and `LICENSE.quickjs` (the upstream `LICENSE`).

To update, replace these files with the ones of the new release, review the
source list in `CMakeLists.txt` against the upstream `Makefile` and run the
tests.

## References

- **QuickJS** documentation [HTML version](https://bellard.org/quickjs/quickjs.html), [PDF version](https://bellard.org/quickjs/quickjs.pdf).
- **QuickJS** [source repository](https://github.com/bellard/quickjs).
- [Writing native modules in C for QuickJS](https://medium.com/@calbertts/writing-native-modules-in-c-for-quickjs-engine-49043587f2e2).
- [How to create asynchronous code for QuickJS](https://medium.com/@calbertts/how-to-create-asynchronous-apis-for-quickjs-8aca5488bb2e).

# quickjs-build changelog

## 2026-11-15 Version 7.0.0, @NickNaso

### Notable changes

* Update QuickJS to version 2026-06-04. The engine now supports most of ES2025:
  top-level await, WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry, iterator helpers, the Set
  methods, resizable ArrayBuffer, the RegExp `v` flag and modifiers,
  Float16Array, JSON modules with import attributes, `Promise.try`,
  `Math.sumPrecise` and more.
* The release archives are cross-compiled with `zig cc` from one Linux runner:
  13 native platforms instead of 5, plus WebAssembly (`wasm32-wasi` and
  `wasm32-emscripten`, engine only).
* New `qjs-windows-x86_64-mingw.zip` and `qjs-windows-x86-mingw.zip` archives,
  built natively on Windows with MinGW-w64 11 (MinGW-Builds GCC 13.2, msvcrt):
  they link with MinGW-w64 toolchains that cannot link the zig archives,
  including releases older than 12.
* The Linux archives no longer depend on the Ubuntu version of the CI runner:
  they need glibc 2.17 or later (2.27 for RISC-V). Static musl builds are also
  provided.
* New CMake options `QJS_BUILD_LIBC`, `QJS_BUILD_TOOLS`, `QJS_BUILD_SMOKE_TEST`
  and `QJSC_EXECUTABLE`; new `check` target that runs the QuickJS tests.
* New CMake toolchain file `toolchains/zig.cmake` and build script
  `scripts/build.sh`. `toolchains/linux_aarch64.cmake` and the dependency on
  qemu to build for arm64 were removed.
* The CI runs the tests on Linux x86_64, x86, arm64, armv7 and riscv64 and on
  real Windows and macOS runners, and publishes a `SHA256SUMS` file with every
  release.

### Breaking changes

#### QuickJS API

* The mathematical extensions were removed upstream: `CONFIG_BIGNUM`,
  `libbf`, `qjscalc`, BigFloat, BigDecimal and operator overloading are gone,
  together with `JS_AddIntrinsicBigFloat`, `JS_AddIntrinsicBigDecimal`,
  `JS_AddIntrinsicOperators`, `JS_EnableBignumExt`, `JS_IsBigFloat` and
  `JS_IsBigDecimal`. BigInt is always available and `JS_AddIntrinsicBigInt`
  no longer exists.
* `JS_EVAL_FLAG_STRIP` was removed: use `JS_SetStripInfo`.
* `JS_ResetUncatchableError` was removed: use `JS_SetUncatchableException`.
* `JS_RunModule` was removed: use `JS_LoadModule`.
* `JS_PROP_NO_ADD`, `JS_VALUE_GET_OBJ` and `JS_VALUE_GET_STRING` were removed
  from `quickjs.h`.
* `JS_SetPropertyInternal` has an additional `this_obj` parameter.
* `js_module_loader` (`quickjs-libc.h`) has an additional
  `JSValueConst attributes` parameter.
* The `JS_AddIntrinsic*` functions, `JS_SetConstructor` and
  `JS_SetPropertyFunctionList` now return `int` instead of `void`.

#### Archives

* The archives were renamed:

  | 6.0.0 | 7.0.0 |
  | --- | --- |
  | `qjs-windows.zip` | `qjs-windows-x86_64.zip` |
  | `qjs-ubuntu-18_04.zip`, `qjs-ubuntu-20_04.zip` | `qjs-linux-x86_64.zip` |
  | `qjs-linux-arm64.zip` | `qjs-linux-arm64.zip` |
  | `qjs-macOS.zip` | `qjs-macos-x86_64.zip`, `qjs-macos-arm64.zip` |

* The `qjs-windows-*.zip` archives are built with zig against the UCRT and a
  recent MinGW-w64. MinGW-w64 toolchains older than 12 cannot link them
  (undefined references to `pthread_cond_timedwait64` and `clock_gettime64`):
  use the `qjs-windows-*-mingw.zip` archives (msvcrt) instead.
* Every archive now contains `VERSION` and the QuickJS `LICENSE`.

#### Build

* CMake 3.20 or later is required.
* `CONFIG_BIGNUM` is no longer defined for the users of the `qjs` target.
* Cross-compiling the tools requires `-DQJSC_EXECUTABLE=<host qjsc>`.

projects.readme:
# quickjs-napi

[![CI](https://github.com/napi-bindings/quickjs-napi/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=napi)](https://github.com/napi-bindings/quickjs-napi/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

Node-API implementation for [QuickJS](https://bellard.org/quickjs/)
(2026-06-04, from `../quickjs-build`). Addons built for Node.js (node-gyp,
node-addon-api, napi-rs) are loaded **unchanged**: they resolve `napi_*` from
the `quickjs-napi` executable, exactly as they do from `node`.

```sh
quickjs-napi -e "console.log(require('./build/Release/addon.node').hello())"
```

## Status

Milestone **M6** in progress (real-world conformance). Done: M1 values,
strings, objects, properties, functions, classes, errors; M2 references,
externals, wrapping, finalizers, type tags, instance data, `napi_run_script`;
M3 ArrayBuffer, TypedArray, DataView, BigInt, Date, Promise; M4 the
synchronous `node_api.h` (Buffer, async context, `napi_make_callback`,
callback scopes, `napi_fatal_exception`); M5 the libuv event loop (async
work, thread-safe functions, async cleanup hooks,
`napi_get_uv_event_loop`). See `PIANO-IMPLEMENTAZIONE.md` in the project for
the plan.

- All **155 Node-API functions** (version 10) are implemented.
- They pass 30 tests of the Node.js `js-native-api` suite, 19 of its
  `node-api` suite, and 78 of the 83 test modules of the **node-addon-api
  8.9.2** suite in its four binding variants (the others need
  `worker_threads`, `npm` or test the npm package itself).
- Behaviour follows **Node.js 22.23.4**; the few differences are listed in
  [compatibility.md](doc/compatibility.md). `NAPI_EXPERIMENTAL` APIs are not
  provided.

## Quick start

`quickjs-build` must be checked out next to this repository
(`../quickjs-build`, branch `feat/quickjs-2026-06-04`).

```sh
cmake --preset unix-debug            # windows-zig-debug on Windows
cmake --build --preset unix-debug
ctest --preset unix-debug
```

```sh
quickjs-napi [options] script.js [args...]
quickjs-napi [options] -e <code> [args...]
```

Details: [building](doc/building.md), [the executable](doc/host.md).

## Documentation

| Document | Contents |
|---|---|
| [Architecture](doc/architecture.md) | goals, components, host and env, handle-scope arena, function calls, error model, object lifetime on a reference-counting engine, event loop, addon loading, teardown, design decisions; with diagrams |
| [Embedding API](doc/embedding.md) | `qjsnapi.h`: embedding the library in a QuickJS application, every `qjsnapi_*` function, embedder responsibilities, symbol export |
| [Node-API reference](doc/node-api/README.md) | conventions (statuses, pending exceptions, threads), writing an addon, and an index of all 155 functions |
| ↳ [Environment](doc/node-api/environment.md) | last error, versions, module file name, cleanup hooks, `napi_fatal_error`, legacy registration |
| ↳ [Values](doc/node-api/values.md) | singletons, numbers, booleans, `typeof`, coercion, arrays, strict equality |
| ↳ [Strings](doc/node-api/strings.md) | latin1 / UTF-8 / UTF-16 strings, external strings, property keys, symbols |
| ↳ [Objects](doc/node-api/objects.md) | properties by key, name and index, `napi_define_properties`, key enumeration, prototype, freeze/seal, `instanceof` |
| ↳ [Functions](doc/node-api/functions.md) | native functions, `napi_get_cb_info`, calls, `new.target`, classes, `napi_run_script` |
| ↳ [Errors](doc/node-api/errors.md) | error objects, throwing, pending exceptions |
| ↳ [Handle scopes](doc/node-api/scopes.md) | handle and escapable scopes |
| ↳ [Lifetime](doc/node-api/lifetime.md) | references, wrapping, finalizers, externals, type tags, instance data, external memory |
| ↳ [Binary data](doc/node-api/binary-data.md) | ArrayBuffer, TypedArray, DataView, BigInt, Date, Promise |
| ↳ [Node.js-specific](doc/node-api/node-specific.md) | Buffer, async context, `napi_make_callback`, callback scopes, `napi_fatal_exception` |
| ↳ [Asynchronous APIs](doc/node-api/async.md) | async work, thread-safe functions, `napi_get_uv_event_loop` |
| [The executable](doc/host.md) | command line, `NODE_OPTIONS`, CommonJS modules, globals, builtin modules, `child_process`, event loop, exit |
| [Building](doc/building.md) | prerequisites, presets, options, Windows (zig, MSYS2), build outputs, installing, release packages, CI |
| [Testing](doc/testing.md) | test suites, Node.js parity, sanitizers, tools, development workflows |
| [Compatibility](doc/compatibility.md) | every known difference from Node.js 22 |

Test-suite specific notes: [test/node/README.md](test/node/README.md)
(Node.js conformance tests) and
[test/node-addon-api/harness/README.md](test/node-addon-api/harness/README.md)
(node-addon-api suite).

## Repository layout

| Path | |

| `include/` | Node-API headers (v10), QuickJS headers, `qjsnapi.h` |
| `src/env.c` | host and env lifecycle, last error, cleanup hooks |
| `src/lifetime.c` | references, externals, wrap, finalizers and their queue, type tags, instance data |
| `src/scope.c` | handle-scope arena (`napi_value` = pointer to an owned `JSValue` slot) |
| `src/function.c` | functions with `new.target` support (class with a `call` hook), calls, `napi_define_class`, `napi_run_script` |
| `src/value.c` | primitives, numbers, coercion, arrays, strict equality |
| `src/string.c` | strings (latin1/UTF-8/UTF-16, lossless through WTF-8/CESU-8), property keys, symbols |
| `src/object.c` | properties, `napi_define_properties`, property names, prototype, freeze/seal, `instanceof` |
| `src/error.c` | errors and exceptions |
| `src/builtins.c` | ArrayBuffer, TypedArray, DataView, BigInt, Date, Promise/deferred |
| `src/buffer.c`, `src/buffer.js` | Buffer APIs and the minimal Buffer class (embedded at build time) |
| `src/node_api.c` | async context, `napi_make_callback`, callback scopes, `napi_fatal_exception`, the frame of loop-originated callbacks |
| `src/loop.c` | libuv loop ownership, finalizer check/idle handles, drain and close at teardown, `napi_get_uv_event_loop` |
| `src/async.c` | `napi_async_work` on the libuv thread pool |
| `src/tsfn.c` | thread-safe functions |
| `src/loader.c` | `.node` loading: `napi_register_module_v1`, API version, legacy `napi_module_register` |
| `src/stubs_generated.c` | generated by `tools/gen_stubs.py`, do not edit (empty now: every function is implemented) |
| `host/main.c`, `host/bootstrap.js` | the `quickjs-napi` executable: options, event loop, CommonJS loader, `process` and builtin modules (`bootstrap.js` embedded at build time by `cmake/embed.cmake`) |
| `host/spawn.c` | child processes (`spawnSync` on a private loop, `spawn` on the main one) |
| `test/addons`, `test/js` | our test addons; the JS tests also run under Node.js as reference |
| `test/node` | Node.js conformance tests (vendored) |
| `test/node-addon-api` | node-addon-api headers and test suite (vendored by `tools/sync_node_addon_api.py`); `harness/` is ours |
| `test/unit` | C embedding test (teardown order, scopes, error state, finalizer queue) |
| `test/package` | checks an installed / released package (`smoke.sh`, used by the release workflow) |
| `test/lsan.supp` | LeakSanitizer suppressions for leaks the Node.js and node-addon-api tests make by design |
| `cmake/node_addon_api_tests.cmake` | builds the 8 node-addon-api test bindings, one CTest per test module |
| `cmake/expect_abort.cmake` | runs a Node.js test that must abort (`napi_fatal_error`) and checks its output |
| `tools/` | stub generation, export check, test vendoring ([testing.md](doc/testing.md#tools)) |
| `doc/` | this documentation |

docs.markdown:
# Node-API reference

quickjs-napi implements all **155 functions** of Node-API version 10
(`include/js_native_api.h` and `include/node_api.h`, the headers of Node.js
22). This reference documents what each function does **in quickjs-napi**:
its contract, the statuses it returns, and where its behaviour depends on the
QuickJS implementation. The upstream
[Node-API documentation](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/n-api.html)
remains the normative text; differences from Node.js are collected in
[compatibility.md](../compatibility.md).

- [Conventions](#conventions)
- [Writing an addon](#writing-an-addon)
- [Function index](#function-index)

| Area | File | Functions |
|---|---|---|
| Environment, versions, cleanup hooks, module registration | [environment.md](environment.md) | 10 |
| Primitives, numbers, booleans, coercion, arrays | [values.md](values.md) | 24 |
| Strings, property keys, symbols | [strings.md](strings.md) | 13 |
| Objects and properties | [objects.md](objects.md) | 19 |
| Functions, calls, classes, scripts | [functions.md](functions.md) | 7 |
| Errors and exceptions | [errors.md](errors.md) | 12 |
| Handle scopes | [scopes.md](scopes.md) | 5 |
| References, externals, wrap, finalizers, type tags, instance data | [lifetime.md](lifetime.md) | 16 |
| ArrayBuffer, TypedArray, DataView, BigInt, Date, Promise | [binary-data.md](binary-data.md) | 25 |
| Buffer, async context, `napi_make_callback`, callback scopes | [node-specific.md](node-specific.md) | 12 |
| Async work, thread-safe functions, the event loop | [async.md](async.md) | 12 |

## Conventions

### Status codes and the last error

Every function returns a `napi_status`. `napi_ok` means success; anything else
is a failure and is also recorded as the env's last error, which
`napi_get_last_error_info` returns with a message:

| Status | Message | Typical cause |
|---|---|---|
| `napi_ok` | | success |
| `napi_invalid_arg` | Invalid argument | a `NULL` pointer argument, an out-of-range enum, a value of the wrong kind where no specific status exists |
| `napi_object_expected` | An object was expected | the receiver is `null`/`undefined` (a `TypeError` is then pending), or not an object |
| `napi_string_expected` | A string was expected | |
| `napi_name_expected` | A string or symbol was expected | property keys, symbol descriptions |
| `napi_function_expected` | A function was expected | |
| `napi_number_expected` | A number was expected | getters never coerce |
| `napi_boolean_expected` | A boolean was expected | |
| `napi_array_expected` | An array was expected | |
| `napi_generic_failure` | Unknown failure | out of memory, or a failed engine operation without a JS exception |
| `napi_pending_exception` | An exception is pending | JavaScript threw during the call, or an exception was already pending |
| `napi_cancelled` | The async work item was cancelled | passed to `complete` |
| `napi_escape_called_twice` | napi_escape_handle already called on scope | |
| `napi_handle_scope_mismatch` | Invalid handle scope usage | closing a scope that is not the innermost one |
| `napi_callback_scope_mismatch` | Invalid callback scope usage | |
| `napi_queue_full` | Thread-safe function queue is full | non-blocking call on a full queue |
| `napi_closing` | Thread-safe function handle is closing | |
| `napi_bigint_expected` | A bigint was expected | |
| `napi_date_expected` | A date was expected | |
| `napi_arraybuffer_expected` | An arraybuffer was expected | |
| `napi_detachable_arraybuffer_expected` | A detachable arraybuffer was expected | |
| `napi_would_deadlock` | Main thread would deadlock | never returned (as in Node.js 22) |
| `napi_no_external_buffers_allowed` | External buffers are not allowed | never returned: external buffers are always allowed |
| `napi_cannot_run_js` | Cannot run JavaScript | the env is tearing down (modules built for Node-API ≥ 10) |

### Functions that run JavaScript

Some functions may call into JavaScript (getters, setters, `valueOf`,
proxies, user callbacks). These **refuse to start** when an exception is
already pending (`napi_pending_exception`) or when the env can no longer run
JavaScript (`napi_cannot_run_js`, or `napi_pending_exception` for modules
built for Node-API < 10). They are marked **JS** in the
[function index](#function-index). The other functions only touch C
bookkeeping or create values, and work even with an exception pending: this
is what lets an addon build an error message while an exception is pending.

When JavaScript throws during a call, the function returns
`napi_pending_exception` and **the exception stays pending**, exactly as in
Node.js. Returning from the native callback then propagates it to the
JavaScript caller. Use `napi_is_exception_pending` and
`napi_get_and_clear_last_exception` to handle it in C.

### Basic env

Functions whose first parameter is `node_api_basic_env` (cleanup hooks,
instance data, `napi_delete_reference`, `napi_adjust_external_memory`,
`napi_get_uv_event_loop`, ...) may be called from a *basic finalizer*
(`node_api_basic_finalize`). In quickjs-napi every finalizer, basic or not,
runs **outside the garbage collector** (from the event loop or at teardown),
so calling other functions from a basic finalizer never causes the fatal
error Node.js raises; the distinction is kept for source compatibility.

### Values and threads

- A `napi_value` is valid until the handle scope it was created in is closed.
  Values created in a native callback are released when the callback returns,
  unless they are returned, escaped, or kept in a `napi_ref`.
- Every function except the thread-safe function ones
  (`napi_call_threadsafe_function`, `napi_acquire_threadsafe_function`,
  `napi_release_threadsafe_function`,
  `napi_get_threadsafe_function_context`) must be called on the thread that
  runs the event loop. `execute` callbacks of async work run on the thread
  pool and must not call Node-API functions that take an env.

## Writing an addon

Addons are written exactly as for Node.js. A minimal C addon:

```c
#include <node_api.h>

#define NAPI_CALL(env, call)                                            \
  do {                                                                  \
    if ((call) != napi_ok) {                                            \
      const napi_extended_error_info *info;                             \
      bool pending;                                                     \
      napi_get_last_error_info((env), &info);                           \
      napi_is_exception_pending((env), &pending);                       \
      if (!pending)                                                     \
        napi_throw_error((env), NULL, info->error_message               \
                                          ? info->error_message         \
                                          : "Node-API call failed");    \
      return NULL;                                                      \
    }                                                                   \
  } while (0)

static napi_value Add(napi_env env, napi_callback_info info) {
  size_t argc = 2;
  napi_value argv[2];
  NAPI_CALL(env, napi_get_cb_info(env, info, &argc, argv, NULL, NULL));
  double a, b;
  NAPI_CALL(env, napi_get_value_double(env, argv[0], &a));
  NAPI_CALL(env, napi_get_value_double(env, argv[1], &b));
  napi_value sum;
  NAPI_CALL(env, napi_create_double(env, a + b, &sum));
  return sum;
}

NAPI_MODULE_INIT(/* napi_env env, napi_value exports */) {
  napi_property_descriptor desc = {"add", NULL, Add, NULL, NULL, NULL,
                                   napi_default, NULL};
  NAPI_CALL(env, napi_define_properties(env, exports, 1, &desc));
  return exports;
}
```

Build it with node-gyp, cmake-js or any toolchain that produces a Node.js
addon, then:

```sh
quickjs-napi -e "console.log(require('./build/Release/addon.node').add(2, 3))"
```

The same binary loads in Node.js. node-addon-api (C++) and napi-rs (Rust)
addons work the same way; the node-addon-api 8.9.2 test suite runs in CI
([testing.md](../testing.md)).

The module API version is chosen by the addon at build time (`NAPI_VERSION`,
exported through `node_api_module_get_api_version_v1`). It is 8 when the
addon does not declare one, and changes a few behaviours: which values
`napi_create_reference` accepts, the status of
[functions that run JavaScript](#functions-that-run-javascript) during
teardown, and the [thread-safe function exception policy](async.md#exceptions-in-call_js_cb).

## Function index

pending (see [above](#functions-that-run-javascript)).

# Architecture This document explains how quickjs-napi is built and why. It is meant for contributors and for embedders who need to understand what happens behind the Node-API calls. The API itself is described in the [Node-API reference](node-api/README.md) and the [embedding guide](embedding.md). - [Goals and constraints](#goals-and-constraints) - [Components](#components) - [Host and env](#host-and-env) - [Values and handle scopes](#values-and-handle-scopes) - [Calling native functions](#calling-native-functions) - [Errors and exceptions](#errors-and-exceptions) - [Object lifetime](#object-lifetime) - [The event loop](#the-event-loop) - [Loading addons](#loading-addons) - [Teardown](#teardown) - [Captured builtins](#captured-builtins) - [Design decisions](#design-decisions) ## Goals and constraints quickjs-napi implements Node-API (version 10) on top of the [QuickJS](https://bellard.org/quickjs/) engine, so that addons compiled for Node.js load **unchanged**. Everything in the design follows from that goal: 1. **Binary compatibility.** An addon built by node-gyp, node-addon-api or napi-rs does not link against any quickjs-napi library: it resolves the `napi_*` (and `uv_*`) symbols from the running process, exactly as it does from `node`. The executable must therefore export the whole Node-API and libuv. 2. **Observable Node.js semantics.** The reference is Node.js **22.23.4** (`src/js_native_api_v8.cc`, `src/node_api.cc`). Status codes, pending exceptions, property order, error messages and finalizer timing follow it. Each difference is a documented deviation (see [compatibility.md](compatibility.md)). 3. **QuickJS as it is.** The engine is used through its public C API (`quickjs.h`); it is not patched. When QuickJS lacks something V8 has (weak callbacks, `new.target` in C functions, a class ID enum, DataView accessors), the library builds it from what QuickJS has. The main difference between the two engines is the memory model: **V8 uses a tracing GC**, so an object stays alive until a collection finds it unreachable. **QuickJS uses reference counting** plus a cycle collector, so an object is freed as soon as its last reference goes away. Much of the lifetime machinery below exists to make reference counting look like a tracing GC to addons. ## Components ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph process["quickjs-napi process"] direction TB script["user script
(CommonJS)"] boot["host/bootstrap.js
require, process, timers,
Buffer, child_process, ..."] main["host/main.c + host/spawn.c
CLI, event loop phases,
natives for bootstrap.js"] lib["libqjsnapi (src/*.c)
Node-API 10 + qjsnapi.h"] qjs["QuickJS
(libqjs, quickjs-libc)"] uv["libuv 1.51
(static, uv_a)"] script --> boot --> main main --> lib lib --> qjs lib --> uv main --> qjs main --> uv end addon["addon.node
(node-gyp / node-addon-api / napi-rs)"] addon -. "napi_* resolved
from the executable" .-> lib addon -. "uv_*" .-> uv ``` | Component | Role | |---|---| | `src/` (library `qjsnapi`) | The Node-API implementation and the embedding API `include/qjsnapi.h`. It does not depend on the executable and can be embedded in any QuickJS application. | | `host/` (executable `quickjs-napi`) | A small Node.js-like runtime around the library: command line, CommonJS loader, `process`, timers, the event loop. It runs addons and the test suites. See [host.md](host.md). | | QuickJS | Built as a subproject from `../quickjs-build`. `include/quickjs.h` must match it exactly (the `JSValue` ABI); configuration fails otherwise. | | libuv | Fetched at configure time (v1.51.0), built statically and exported by the executable, because addons call `uv_*` directly. | The library is linked into the executable as a **whole archive** (`QJSNAPI_WHOLE_ARCHIVE` in `CMakeLists.txt`), so that the objects of functions the host itself never calls are kept and exported too. The `exports_complete` test (`tools/check_exports.py`) checks that all 155 functions are exported. ### Source layout of the library | File | Responsibility | Node-API functions | |---|---|---| | `env.c` | host and env lifecycle, last error, cleanup hooks, versions, fatal errors | 9 | | `scope.c` | handle-scope arena | 5 | | `value.c` | singletons, numbers, booleans, `typeof`, coercion, arrays, strict equality | 24 | | `string.c` | strings (latin1, UTF-8, UTF-16), property keys, symbols | 13 | | `object.c` | properties, descriptors, key enumeration, prototype, freeze/seal, `instanceof` | 19 | | `function.c` | functions, calls, `new.target`, classes, `napi_run_script` | 7 | | `error.c` | error objects and exceptions | 12 | | `lifetime.c` | references, externals, wrap, finalizers, type tags, instance data | 16 | | `builtins.c` | ArrayBuffer, TypedArray, DataView, BigInt, Date, Promise | 25 | | `buffer.c`, `buffer.js` | Node.js `Buffer` | 6 | | `node_api.c` | async context, `napi_make_callback`, callback scopes, `napi_fatal_exception` | 6 | | `async.c` | async work on the libuv thread pool | 4 | | `tsfn.c` | thread-safe functions | 7 | | `loop.c` | libuv loop ownership, finalizer handles, `napi_get_uv_event_loop` | 1 | | `loader.c` | `.node` loading, legacy `napi_module_register` | 1 | | `stubs_generated.c` | generated stubs for unimplemented functions (empty: everything is implemented) | 0 | Shared types and helpers live in `src/qjsnapi_internal.h`. Internal functions carry the `qn_` prefix and are hidden (`QN_INTERNAL`, ELF visibility `hidden`), so the only exported symbols are the Node-API and `qjsnapi_*` ones. ## Host and env Node.js has one *environment* per thread and one `napi_env` per loaded addon. quickjs-napi keeps the same split: ```mermaid classDiagram direction LR class JSRuntime class JSContext { opaque points to the host } class qjsnapi_host { uv_loop_t* loop qn_list envs qn_list modules JSValue holders (WeakMap) captured builtins JSValue* kept uncaught / checkpoint callbacks } class napi_env__ { int32 module_api_version bool can_call_into_js last_error qn_arena arena cleanup_hooks reflist / finalizing_reflist pending_finalizers works, deferreds, async_contexts } class qn_module_record { path dlopen handle legacy napi_module } JSRuntime "1" o-- "1..*" JSContext JSContext "1" -- "1" qjsnapi_host qjsnapi_host "1" *-- "*" napi_env__ : one per addon load qjsnapi_host "1" *-- "*" qn_module_record qn_module_record --> napi_env__ ``` - **`qjsnapi_host`** (one per `JSContext`, stored as the context opaque) owns everything that is shared: the libuv loop, the captured builtins, the `WeakMap` of lifetime holders, the list of envs and loaded modules, the *kept objects* list, and the embedder's callbacks (uncaught exception handler, checkpoint). - **`napi_env__`** (one per addon initialization) owns what Node.js keeps per module: the **module API version** (which changes some behaviours, e.g. `napi_cannot_run_js` instead of `napi_pending_exception` during teardown), the last error, the handle-scope arena, cleanup hooks, references, the finalizer queue, and the async objects not yet released. Loading the same addon twice creates two envs, like `process.dlopen` in Node.js: the initializer runs again and returns new exports. ## Values and handle scopes A `napi_value` is an opaque pointer. In quickjs-napi it **points to a `JSValue` slot** in an arena owned by the env. Each slot owns exactly one QuickJS reference (`JS_DupValue` when the slot is filled, `JS_FreeValue` when its scope closes). This is the reference-counting equivalent of a V8 local handle. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph arena["env arena: chunks of 256 JSValue slots, never moved"] direction LR c1["chunk 1
slots 0..255"] --- c2["chunk 2
slots 0..255"] --- c3["chunk 3
..."] end root["root scope
mark: chunk 1, slot 0"] -.-> c1 s1["implicit scope of a call
mark: chunk 1, slot 17"] -.-> c1 s2["napi_open_handle_scope
mark: chunk 2, slot 40"] -.-> c2 top["top: next free slot"] -.-> c3 ``` - Slots are allocated by bumping `arena.top`. Chunks are linked, never reallocated, so a `napi_value` stays valid until its scope closes. - A scope records the arena position (`qn_mark`) when it opens. Closing it frees, in LIFO order, every slot allocated since then and resets `top`. Closing a scope is O(number of values created in it), with no per-handle bookkeeping. - **Escapable scopes** reserve one slot in the parent *before* recording their own mark. `napi_escape_handle` stores a duplicated reference into that slot, so the value survives the inner scope. Escaping twice returns `napi_escape_called_twice`. - Every native entry point (a function call, a finalizer, module init, a loop callback) runs inside an **implicit scope**, so addons that never open scopes do not leak. Closing a scope that is not the innermost one returns `napi_handle_scope_mismatch`. - Scope records are recycled through a free list, so opening a scope does not allocate in the steady state. ## Calling native functions `JS_NewCFunctionData` is not enough for Node-API: its trampoline does not expose `new.target`, which `napi_get_new_target` and `napi_define_class` need. Native functions are therefore objects of a dedicated QuickJS class with a `call` hook. QuickJS passes `JS_CALL_FLAG_CONSTRUCTOR` and, for construct calls, `new.target` as `this_val`. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant JS as JavaScript participant T as qn_function_call (trampoline) participant S as handle-scope arena participant CB as addon callback JS->>T: f(a, b) or new F(a, b) alt construct call T->>T: receiver = object with new.target.prototype else plain call T->>T: receiver = this end T->>S: open implicit scope T->>T: clear last error, native_depth++ T->>CB: cb(env, &callback_info) CB->>S: napi_create_* (new slots) CB-->>T: napi_value result (or NULL) T->>T: native_depth-- alt exception pending T-->>JS: JS_EXCEPTION (the exception propagates) else T->>T: duplicate the result out of the scope end T->>S: close the scope (frees every slot of the call) T-->>JS: result, or the receiver when a construct call
returned a non-object ``` - `napi_callback_info` points to a stack record (`this`, `new.target`, `argc`, `argv`, `data`): there is no allocation per call. - The per-function record (`qn_function`: env, callback, data) is owned by the function object and freed by its class finalizer. It holds no `JSValue`, so the class needs no `gc_mark` hook. - `host->native_depth` counts the native frames on the stack. It is `0` only when no JavaScript is below the running native code, which is how callback scopes decide whether to run a microtask checkpoint. - A function whose env is shutting down throws an `InternalError` instead of calling into the addon. `napi_define_class` creates such a function and defines the instance properties on its `prototype` and the static ones on the constructor. As with V8's prototype templates, a later instance property with the same key replaces an earlier one regardless of its attributes. ## Errors and exceptions Node-API reports errors in two ways, and quickjs-napi keeps both exactly like Node.js: 1. **Status codes.** Every function returns a `napi_status` and records it as the env's *last error* (`napi_get_last_error_info`). The checks are the macros of `qjsnapi_internal.h`, named after their Node.js equivalents: `CHECK_ENV`, `CHECK_ARG`, `RETURN_STATUS_IF_FALSE`, `NAPI_PREAMBLE`, `CHECK_JS`, `GET_RETURN_STATUS`. 2. **JavaScript exceptions.** QuickJS keeps the pending exception on the runtime. A JavaScript failure leaves it pending, exactly like V8, and the function returns `napi_pending_exception`. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["API that may run JavaScript"] --> P{"NAPI_PREAMBLE"} P -- "env is NULL" --> E1["napi_invalid_arg"] P -- "an exception is already pending" --> E2["napi_pending_exception"] P -- "env is tearing down" --> E3["napi_cannot_run_js (module API >= 10)
napi_pending_exception (older modules)"] P -- ok --> B["clear the last error, run the QuickJS call"] B -- "JavaScript threw" --> E4["napi_pending_exception
(the exception stays pending)"] B -- "other failure" --> E5["specific status
(napi_*_expected, napi_generic_failure, ...)"] B -- ok --> OK["napi_ok"] ``` When a native callback returns with an exception pending, the trampoline returns `JS_EXCEPTION`, so the exception propagates to the JavaScript caller. When there is no JavaScript caller (a finalizer, an async work completion, a thread-safe function call), the exception goes to the host's **uncaught handler** (`qjsnapi_host_set_uncaught_handler`), which the executable maps to `process.on('uncaughtException')`. ## Object lifetime This is where the two engines differ most. The [lifetime reference](node-api/lifetime.md) describes the API; this section explains the mechanism. ### References `napi_ref` (`struct napi_ref__`) mirrors `v8impl::Reference`: ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Strong: create with count > 0 [*] --> Weak: create with count 0
(object, function, local symbol) [*] --> Empty: create with count 0
(any other value) Strong --> Weak: unref reaches 0, weakable target Strong --> Empty: unref reaches 0, other value Weak --> Strong: ref, target still alive Weak --> Empty: target collected (holder finalizer) Strong --> [*]: napi_delete_reference Weak --> [*]: napi_delete_reference Empty --> [*]: napi_delete_reference ``` - **Strong** (count > 0): the reference owns a `JSValue`. - **Weak** (count 0; object, function or non-registered symbol): it holds a JavaScript `WeakRef`. QuickJS reports a `WeakRef` target dead as soon as its refcount drops to zero, so `napi_get_reference_value` returns `NULL` exactly when the value is gone. The target is also on the *kept-objects* list until the next clear (see below). - **Empty** (count 0, any other value): the value is released for good, like a reset V8 persistent. - Registered symbols (`Symbol.for`) cannot be held weakly by QuickJS. They are never collected anyway, so they stay strong (`keep_strong`), which is what Node.js observably does. ### Kept objects V8 keeps the target of a weak handle alive until the next GC. node-addon-api relies on this: `Napi::Weak(Object::New(env))` is used later in the same synchronous code. Under reference counting such an object would die when the call's scope closes. So when a reference becomes weak, its target is also put on a **kept-objects list**, like the `[[KeptAlive]]` list of ECMAScript `WeakRef`s. The list is cleared: - at the end of every macrotask (the library's checkpoint, after each callback from the event loop); - by `gc()` in the executable; - by the embedder, with `qjsnapi_host_clear_kept_objects`; - at teardown. ### Weak callbacks through holders V8 notifies a weak persistent when its target is collected; QuickJS has no such hook in its C API. quickjs-napi gets the notification through a **holder**: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant A as addon participant L as lifetime.c participant W as host.holders (WeakMap) participant H as NapiHolder object participant G as QuickJS GC participant Q as env.pending_finalizers participant U as event loop (uv_check) A->>L: napi_wrap / napi_create_reference / napi_type_tag_object L->>W: get(target), or set(target, new holder) L->>H: register the reference, wrap or tag Note over G: the target becomes unreachable G->>W: JS_RunGC drops the entry of the dead key W->>H: the holder is freed H->>L: class finalizer: notify every registered reference L->>Q: no finalizer: reset now
with a finalizer: queue it U->>Q: qjsnapi_host_run_finalizers Q->>A: finalize_cb(env, data, hint) in its own scope ``` - Each target of a reference, wrap or type tag gets **one holder**, an object of the internal `NapiHolder` class stored in `host->holders`, a `WeakMap` keyed by the target. - QuickJS drops the entries of dead keys during `JS_RunGC`. The holder is freed, and its class finalizer plays the role of V8's weak callback. - The holder also stores the `napi_wrap` reference and the type tag, so **wrapping and tagging work on any object** (frozen objects, proxies, functions) without adding properties to it. - QuickJS drops weak entries *before* collecting cycles, so a target that died in a cycle is only seen dead by a second pass: `gc()` runs `JS_RunGC` twice. ### Finalizers are deferred Finalizers **never run inside the GC**. As in Node.js, they are queued on the env (`pending_finalizers`) and run later from the event loop, where JavaScript may run (`qjsnapi_host_run_finalizers`), each in its own handle scope and followed by a checkpoint. Finalizers still queued at teardown run then, with JavaScript disabled (`napi_cannot_run_js`). External values (`napi_create_external`), external ArrayBuffers and external Buffers use the same queue: their finalizer runs after the object is collected, never synchronously. ## The event loop The host is bound to a **libuv loop**: `qjsnapi_host_create` creates its own, `qjsnapi_host_create_with_loop` uses the embedder's. The library only adds handles to the loop; **the embedder runs it** (`uv_run`). ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph iteration["one libuv iteration"] direction LR T["timers"] --> P["pending"] --> I["idle / prepare"] --> PO["poll (I/O)"] --> C["check"] --> CL["close callbacks"] end W["async work completion
(uv_queue_work after_work)"] -.-> PO TS["thread-safe function dispatch
(uv_async_t)"] -.-> PO FI["finalizer_idle (uv_idle_t)
active while finalizers are queued,
so poll does not block"] -.-> I FC["finalizer_check (uv_check_t, unreferenced)
runs the queued finalizers"] -.-> C ``` | Handle | Owner | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `finalizer_check` (`uv_check_t`, unreferenced) | `loop.c` | runs the queued finalizers at the end of each iteration, then a checkpoint | | `finalizer_idle` (`uv_idle_t`) | `loop.c` | active only while finalizers are queued: keeps the loop alive and stops the poll phase from blocking (Node.js uses a referenced `SetImmediate`) | | `uv_work_t` per queued work item | `async.c` | `execute` on the thread pool, `complete` on the loop thread | | `uv_async_t` per thread-safe function | `tsfn.c` | wakes the loop thread to dispatch queued calls (referenced unless `napi_unref_threadsafe_function`) | Every callback from the loop into native code goes through a **callback frame** (`qn_callback_enter` / `qn_callback_leave`): a handle scope, a callback scope, and on exit an exception check (reported as uncaught) and, for the outermost scope, a **checkpoint**. The default checkpoint runs the pending promise jobs (`JS_ExecutePendingJob`); the embedder can replace it (`qjsnapi_host_set_checkpoint`) to drain its own queues too, which is what the executable does for `process.nextTick` and unhandled rejections. ### Async work ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant A as addon (loop thread) participant L as libuv loop participant P as thread pool A->>A: napi_create_async_work(execute, complete, data) A->>L: napi_queue_async_work (uv_queue_work), active_works++ L->>P: execute(env, data), no JavaScript allowed P-->>L: done L->>A: after_work: active_works--, then complete(env, napi_ok, data)
inside a callback frame A->>A: napi_delete_async_work (usually from complete) Note over A,L: napi_cancel_async_work before execute starts:
complete(env, napi_cancelled, data) ``` The item is uncounted *before* `complete` runs, so `complete` may queue the same item again. ### Thread-safe functions A port of Node 22's `v8impl::ThreadSafeFunction` on libuv primitives: a mutex, a queue (bounded when `max_queue_size > 0`, with a condition variable for blocked producers), a `uv_async_t` that wakes the loop thread, and at most 1000 calls dispatched per wake-up so that other handles are not starved. ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Open: napi_create_threadsafe_function
(thread_count = initial_thread_count) Open --> Open: call queues an item, acquire increments,
release decrements thread_count Open --> Closing: thread_count reaches 0 and the queue is empty Open --> Closing: release with napi_tsfn_abort Open --> Closing: env teardown (internal cleanup hook) Closing --> Finalized: uv_close callback runs thread_finalize_cb,
then call_js_cb(env = NULL) for each queued item Finalized --> [*] ``` While closing, producers get `napi_closing`. ## Loading addons ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant R as require / embedder participant L as qjsnapi_load_addon participant D as dlopen / LoadLibrary participant M as addon R->>L: path L->>D: open the absolute path (the handle is never closed) D->>M: static constructors run M-->>L: napi_module_register(mod), legacy addons only L->>M: dlsym napi_register_module_v1 L->>M: dlsym node_api_module_get_api_version_v1 (optional) L->>L: version: missing = 8, below 8 raised to 8,
above 10 = ERR_DLOPEN_FAILED L->>L: new env, implicit scope, exports = {} L->>M: init(env, exports) M-->>L: exports, or a replacement value L-->>R: new reference to the exports ``` 1. `node_api_module_get_api_version_v1` (optional, default 8) gives the module API version. A version above 10 is refused with `ERR_DLOPEN_FAILED`; one below 8 is raised to 8, as in Node.js. 2. `napi_register_module_v1` is the symbol-based entry point (what `NAPI_MODULE` and `NAPI_MODULE_INIT` produce). 3. Otherwise, a `napi_module` registered by `napi_module_register()` from a static constructor **during** `dlopen` (legacy addons). The constructor only runs on the first `dlopen` of a file, so the record is remembered and reused by later loads. If the initializer returns a value other than `exports`, that value replaces the exports, as Node.js assigns it to `module.exports`. Library handles are **never closed**: finalizers and cleanup hooks may point into addon code until the very end of the process. Static addons, linked into the embedder, use `qjsnapi_init_static_addon`, which runs the initializer once and caches its exports by name. ## Teardown `qjsnapi_host_destroy` mirrors Node's `Environment::RunCleanup` and `node_napi_env__::DeleteMe`: ```mermaid flowchart TD S["qjsnapi_host_destroy"] --> A["1. every env, newest first:
can_call_into_js = false, then cleanup hooks LIFO
(user hooks, async hooks start, thread-safe functions start closing)"] A --> B["2. queued async work cancelled"] B --> C["3. uv_run(UV_RUN_ONCE) until in-flight work,
closing thread-safe functions and
started async cleanup hooks are done"] C --> D["4. every env, newest first: queued finalizers,
then references with a finalizer (instance data included),
then plain references"] D --> E["5. module cache released (exports objects)"] E --> F["6. every env arena released (all napi_value slots)"] F --> G["7. library loop handles closed (the loop too when owned),
captured builtins released, host detached from the context"] G --> H["embedder: JS_FreeContext, JS_FreeRuntime"] ``` - References with a finalizer are finalized before plain ones, because their finalizers may delete plain references. - Async work items and user references the addon never deleted are freed with the env. Node.js leaks them; here nothing can reach them after teardown, and freeing them keeps the QuickJS leak assertion (`JS_FreeRuntime` in Debug builds) meaningful. - In the executable, `process.exit()` and fatal exceptions **skip** this teardown, as Node.js does: no cleanup hook or finalizer runs. ## Captured builtins Some APIs have no QuickJS C equivalent and are implemented by calling a JavaScript builtin: `WeakRef`, `WeakMap.prototype.get/set`, `Object.freeze`, `Object.seal`, `Symbol`, `Symbol.for`, the `DataView` and `%TypedArray%` getters, `Date.prototype.getTime`, and BigInt conversion to and from hexadecimal. These are captured **when the host is created, before any user script runs**, and stored on the host. Monkey-patching the globals later therefore cannot change what Node-API reports, which matches V8, where these operations do not go through JavaScript. QuickJS does not export its class ID enum. The class IDs of `ArrayBuffer`, `SharedArrayBuffer`, `DataView`, `Date` and the 12 typed arrays are found by **probing one instance of each** at startup (`host->cid_*`); type checks then compare class IDs. ## Design decisions | Decision | Alternative | Why | |---|---|---| | Addons resolve `napi_*` from the executable | ship a `libnode`-like shared library | It is how addons are built for Node.js. Prebuilt binaries work unchanged, including MSVC builds on Windows (node-gyp's delay-load hook redirects the `node.exe` imports to the running process). | | `napi_value` = pointer to an arena slot that owns one reference | box every value in a malloc'ed handle; or cast the `JSValue` itself | A `JSValue` is larger than a pointer on every target (a 16-byte struct on 64-bit, a NaN-boxed 64-bit value on 32-bit). The arena gives stable addresses, O(1) allocation, and scope release without per-handle bookkeeping. | | Weak callbacks through a `WeakMap` of holders | patch QuickJS to add weak callbacks; add hidden properties to the target | Uses only the public API; works on frozen objects, proxies and functions; the engine stays unpatched. | | Kept-objects list for weak targets | pure reference-counting semantics | Without it, objects referenced only weakly die when the creating call returns, which breaks node-addon-api (`Napi::Weak`). The list reproduces V8's "alive until the next GC" the same way ECMAScript `WeakRef` does. | | Finalizers queued and run from the loop | run them in the QuickJS class finalizer | Node.js does the same; a QuickJS class finalizer runs inside the GC, where calling into the engine is unsafe. | | Dedicated function class with a `call` hook | `JS_NewCFunctionData` | Only the `call` hook receives `new.target`, needed by `napi_get_new_target` and `napi_define_class`. | | Builtins captured at startup | look them up on `globalThis` at each call | Immune to monkey-patching, like V8; no lookup per call. | | libuv as the event loop | a custom loop | Addons call `napi_get_uv_event_loop` and `uv_*` directly; the semantics of async work and thread-safe functions are defined in libuv terms. | | Library and executable are separate | a single executable | The library can be embedded in any QuickJS application ([embedding.md](embedding.md)); the executable is one embedder among others. | | Free what the addon leaked at teardown | leak like Node.js | Debug builds of QuickJS assert that every object is released at `JS_FreeRuntime`, which turns any leak in the library into a test failure. | | Node.js 22 as the behavioural reference, checked by running the same JS tests under Node.js | follow the Node-API documentation only | The documentation leaves many details open (property order, error codes, edge cases); the Node.js implementation and its test suites are the contract addons actually depend on. |

docs.title: Building
docs.markdown:
# Building

quickjs-napi builds with CMake (3.24 or newer; 3.25 to use the presets) and
Ninja. It needs the QuickJS sources of `quickjs-build` and fetches libuv at
configure time.

- [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)
- [Presets](#presets)
- [Options](#options)
- [Windows](#windows)
- [What the build produces](#what-the-build-produces)
- [Installing](#installing)
- [Release packages](#release-packages)
- [Continuous integration](#continuous-integration)

## Prerequisites

| Requirement | Notes |
|---|---|
| `quickjs-build` checked out **next to** this repository | `../quickjs-build`, its latest release (7.0.0: QuickJS 2026-06-04); or point `QJSNAPI_QUICKJS_DIR` at it |
| CMake and Ninja | |
| A C17 compiler | gcc or clang on Linux/macOS; zig (`zig cc`) or MSYS2 MinGW on Windows. MSVC is not supported (QuickJS does not build with it) |
| A C++17 compiler | only for the C++ test addons and the node-addon-api suite |
| Network access at configure time | libuv v1.51.0 is fetched with `FetchContent`. Offline: `-DFETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_LIBUV=<libuv checkout>` |
| Node.js 22 (optional) | runs the `node_parity_*` tests, which execute the JS tests under Node.js as a reference |
| Python 3 (optional) | `tools/*.py` (stub generation check, export check, test vendoring) |

`include/quickjs.h` and `include/quickjs-libc.h` must be **identical** to the
ones in `quickjs-build`: configuration fails otherwise, because a different
header means a different `JSValue` ABI.

## Presets

The presets in `CMakePresets.json` are the reference configurations, used by
CI too. Each one builds in `build/<preset>`:

| Preset | Configuration |
|---|---|
| `unix-debug` | Linux/macOS, Debug. QuickJS's leak assertion at `JS_FreeRuntime` is active. |
| `unix-release` | Linux/macOS, Release |
| `unix-asan` | Linux/macOS, Debug + AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, QuickJS included |
| `unix-tsan` | Linux/macOS, Debug + ThreadSanitizer, QuickJS and libuv included |
| `windows-zig-debug`, `windows-zig-release` | Windows x64 with `zig cc` |

```sh
cmake --preset unix-debug
cmake --build --preset unix-debug
ctest --preset unix-debug
```

Without presets:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure
```

### Debug builds and the C stack

With Clang (`zig cc` included), Debug builds compile the **QuickJS library
itself with `-O1`**: at `-O0` its interpreter loop needs about 64 KiB of C
stack per JavaScript call, and QuickJS's 1 MiB stack limit would stop at about
16 nested calls. Our own code keeps the Debug flags, and QuickJS keeps its
assertions.

## Options

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `QJSNAPI_QUICKJS_DIR` | `../quickjs-build` | QuickJS sources, built as a subproject |
| `QJSNAPI_QUICKJS_LIBRARY` | empty | prebuilt `libqjs.a` when the sources are not available |
| `QJSNAPI_SANITIZE` | `OFF` | ASan + UBSan for everything, QuickJS included |
| `QJSNAPI_TSAN` | `OFF` | ThreadSanitizer for everything (exclusive with `QJSNAPI_SANITIZE`) |
| `QJSNAPI_BUILD_TESTS` | `ON` | test addons and the CTest suite |
| `QJSNAPI_NODE_ADDON_API_TESTS` | `ON` | the node-addon-api suite (8 C++ bindings, about 2 minutes of build) |
| `QJSNAPI_BUILD_SHARED` | `ON` | also build the shared library (QuickJS and libuv inside); turns on position-independent code for everything |
| `QJSNAPI_INSTALL_HOST` | `ON` | install the `quickjs-napi` executable |
| `QJSNAPI_QUICKJS_BUILD_REF` | empty | the quickjs-build tag recorded in `BUILDINFO.txt` (set by the release workflow) |

## Windows

QuickJS does not support Microsoft Visual C++: the Visual Studio generators
(and clang-cl) are rejected at configure time. Use a MinGW-w64 toolchain with
Ninja, as quickjs-build does.

### zig

Install the zig version in `../quickjs-build/.zigversion` (for example
`winget install zig.zig`). `zig` must be in `PATH`, or set the `ZIG`
environment variable. Use the presets, which pass the toolchain file:

```sh
cmake --preset windows-zig-debug
cmake --build --preset windows-zig-debug
ctest --preset windows-zig-debug
```

In VS Code (CMake Tools) select the configure preset *Windows x64 - zig -
Debug*. Do **not** use a "zig" compiler *kit*: a kit sets `CMAKE_AR=zig;ar`
without the toolchain file, and Ninja then runs the literal command `zig;ar`
(`error: unknown command: ;ar`). If `build/` still holds a tree configured
with a kit or a Visual Studio generator (`build/CMakeCache.txt`), delete it
once before the first configure.

### MSYS2

From a UCRT64 shell (`pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-{gcc,cmake,ninja}`),
use the generic commands above.

### Addons built with MSVC

Addons compiled with MSVC by node-gyp still load in the MinGW-built
`quickjs-napi.exe`: Node-API is a plain C ABI, and node-gyp's delay-load hook
resolves the `napi_*` imports from the running executable.

## What the build produces

| Target | What it is |
|---|---|
| `qjsnapi` | static library: the Node-API implementation and `qjsnapi.h` |
| `qjsnapi_shared` | shared library `libqjsnapi.so` / `libqjsnapi.dylib` / `qjsnapi.dll`: the same sources plus all of QuickJS and libuv ([embedding.md](embedding.md#from-a-release-package)) |
| `quickjs-napi` | the executable ([host.md](host.md)); exports every `napi_*` and `uv_*` symbol |
| `test_embed` | the C embedding test |
| test addons | `test/addons`, the Node.js conformance addons, the 8 node-addon-api bindings |

Two JavaScript sources are **embedded as C byte arrays** at build time by
`cmake/embed.cmake`: `src/buffer.js` (into the library) and
`host/bootstrap.js` (into the executable). Editing them requires a rebuild,
not a reinstall.

How the executable exports its symbols on each platform (whole archive,
`--export-dynamic`, `__declspec(dllexport)`, `-undefined dynamic_lookup` for
addons on macOS) is described in [embedding.md](embedding.md#linking).

On Windows, QuickJS has no export annotations: `cmake/gen_def.cmake` reads
the symbol index of `libqjs.a` and writes a `.def` file listing its
`JS_*`, `__JS_*` and `js_*` symbols for `qjsnapi.dll` (the zig linker
ignores `--export-all-symbols`).

## Installing

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DQJSNAPI_BUILD_TESTS=OFF       -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=/opt/quickjs-napi
cmake --build build
cmake --install build
```

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| `bin/` | `quickjs-napi`; `qjsnapi.dll` on Windows |
| `include/` | `node_api.h`, `node_api_types.h`, `js_native_api.h`, `js_native_api_types.h`, `qjsnapi.h`, `quickjs.h`, `quickjs-libc.h`, `uv.h`, `uv/*.h` |
| `lib/` | `libqjsnapi.a`, `libqjs.a`, `libuv.a` (three separate archives); `libqjsnapi.so` / `.dylib`; on Windows the import libraries `libqjsnapi.dll.a` (the DLL) and `libquickjs-napi.dll.a` (the executable, for MinGW addons) |
| `lib/cmake/qjsnapi/` | `find_package(qjsnapi)`, targets in [embedding.md](embedding.md#from-a-release-package) |
| `share/doc/quickjs-napi/` | `LICENSE`, `licenses/` (QuickJS, quickjs-build, libuv), `BUILDINFO.txt` (version, target, compiler, QuickJS and libuv versions) |

`test/package/smoke.sh <prefix>` checks an installed tree: it builds
`test/package` with `find_package`, runs the embedding test linked with the
static archives and with the shared library, a script, and the addons of
`test/js/test_hello.js` built with the installed headers only.

## Release packages

`.github/workflows/release.yml` runs when a GitHub release is **published**
(or by hand, `workflow_dispatch`, which does everything but the upload):

1. **prepare**: reads `project(quickjs-napi VERSION x.y.z)` from
   `CMakeLists.txt` and fails if the release tag (`x.y.z` or `vx.y.z`)
   differs; picks the latest release of quickjs-build (or the
   `quickjs_build_ref` input).
2. **ci**: the whole CI suite (`ci.yml`) on that quickjs-build.
3. **build**: one package per platform, Release, tests off, installed and
   zipped as `quickjs-napi-<version>-<platform>.zip` (the layout of
   [Installing](#installing)).
4. **smoke**: `test/package/smoke.sh` on each package, on a machine or
   emulator of its platform.
5. **publish**: only if everything above passed, uploads the zip files and
   `SHA256SUMS` to the release.

| Package | Built with | Smoke test |
|---|---|---|
| `linux-x86_64` | zig, glibc 2.17 | ubuntu, gcc |
| `linux-x86` | zig, glibc 2.17 | ubuntu (32-bit), zig |
| `linux-arm64` | zig, glibc 2.17 | ubuntu arm64, gcc |
| `linux-armv7` | zig, glibc 2.17 | qemu-user |
| `linux-riscv64` | zig, glibc 2.27 | qemu-user |
| `linux-x86_64-musl`, `linux-arm64-musl` | zig, musl | Alpine container, gcc |
| `windows-x86_64`, `windows-x86` | zig, MinGW-w64 UCRT | windows-latest, zig |
| `windows-arm64` | zig, MinGW-w64 UCRT | windows-11-arm, zig |
| `macos-arm64`, `macos-x86_64` | Apple clang, macOS 11+ | native runners |
| `freebsd-x86_64` | zig | compiled and linked only (no hosted FreeBSD runner) |

**musl.** zig links musl executables statically by default, and a static
musl executable cannot `dlopen()` addons. The executable is therefore linked
**dynamically** against the system musl (`/lib/ld-musl-<arch>.so.1`, as on
Alpine); the libraries are the same as for the other platforms. If a musl
smoke test fails because of the executable, set `-DQJSNAPI_INSTALL_HOST=OFF`
for that package in `release.yml`: it then holds the headers and libraries
only (`find_package` reports `QJSNAPI_HAS_HOST` false), for embedders.

**Not packaged:** WebAssembly (no `dlopen`, and libuv does not support WASI),
builds with MSVC (QuickJS does not compile with it; MSVC addons still load in
`quickjs-napi.exe`), Android and iOS.

To release: bump `VERSION` in `CMakeLists.txt`, merge, then publish a
release whose tag is that version.

## Continuous integration

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs on every push and pull request, and from the
release workflow (`workflow_call`). It builds against the latest
quickjs-build release, or the `quickjs_build_ref` input:

| Job | Preset | Compiler |
|---|---|---|
| `linux-gcc-debug` | `unix-debug` | gcc |
| `linux-gcc-release` | `unix-release` | gcc |
| `linux-clang-debug` | `unix-debug` | clang |
| `linux-gcc-asan-ubsan` | `unix-asan` | gcc |
| `linux-gcc-tsan` | `unix-tsan` | gcc |
